item.title: Off-the-Shelf ReaxFF Parameter Sets Underestimate O–O Bond Strengths in Organic Peroxides: A Static and Kinetic Benchmark for Thermal-Hazard Assessment
item.description: ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics (MD) is increasingly used to study organic peroxide decomposition, although the parameter sets supplied with common MD codes were developed for other chemistries. We benchmarked the six C/H/O ReaxFF parameter sets distributed with LAMMPS against CBS-APNO O–O bond dissociation enthalpies (BDEs) of 13 peroxides and tested whether the static error carries over to the kinetics. All six sets underestimate the O–O BDE (mean signed errors of −11.9 to −30.5 kcal mol-1) and correlate only weakly with the references (r = 0.14–0.50). The newer CHO-2016 set (not distributed with LAMMPS) gives −19.5 kcal mol-1, whereas the same protocol yields 85–90 kcal mol-1 for the ethane C–C bond (experiment, about 90 kcal mol-1). The errors increase with alkyl and acyl substitution. For di-tert-butyl peroxide (DTBP), the sets predict 0.4–16.7 instead of 42.4 kcal mol-1, four of them stretch the O–O bond to 1.68–1.76 Å, and a fifth breaks it. Isothermal MD of DTBP at 575–1480 K with three sets gave activation energies of 45.0–76.5 kJ mol-1, consistent with each set’s static BDE (48.7–69.9 kJ mol-1) but 2.0–3.4 times lower than the experimental 153 kJ mol-1. At 121 °C, the extrapolated rate constants exceed manufacturer data by factors of 3.4 × 108 to 5.0 × 1012, and the predicted 10 h half-life temperatures (−147 to −59 °C) lie 180–270 °C below the measured 121 °C. Calculating the O–O BDE of the target peroxide is therefore a simple but necessary check before using a ReaxFF parameter set for hazard assessment.

item.title: Structure-Based Virtual Screening of Enantia chlorantha Stem Bark Constituents Reveals Candidate Pancreatic Alpha-Amylase Inhibitors
item.description: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) remains a major global health burden, and inhibition of pancreatic alpha-amylase is an established strategy for limiting postprandial hyperglycaemia. Enantia chlorantha stem bark is widely used in Nigerian ethnomedicine, but its alpha-amylase-inhibitory phytoconstituents have not been characterised at the molecular level. This study applied structure-based computational screening to identify candidate alpha-amylase inhibitors from E. chlorantha stem bark, using a previously reported GC-MS phytochemical profile of a carbonated stem-bark extract as the source of the screened ligand library. The GC-MS-identified constituents were docked against human pancreatic alpha-amylase (PDB ID: 1B2Y) using Glide, followed by induced fit docking (IFD) of the top-ranked hits and ADMET prediction (SwissADME, ProTox-III). Neoisolongifolene-8-ol emerged as the most promising hit, with a docking score of −6.201 kcal/mol. To assess the physical plausibility of this predicted interaction, a 10 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation of the enzyme–Neoisolongifolene-8-ol complex was performed in GROMACS 2024.5 with the CHARMM36m force field. The complex remained conformationally stable throughout the simulation (mean backbone RMSD = 1.17 ± 0.13 Å; mean radius of gyration = 2.352 ± 0.008 nm), with a well-maintained intramolecular hydrogen-bonding network (384.8 ± 8.7 bonds) and narrow solvent-accessible surface area fluctuation (201.5 ± 2.4 nm2). The ligand hydroxyl group formed a persistent hydrogen bond with the active-site residue His305, and principal component analysis indicated smooth, non-oscillatory conformational sampling consistent with a stable binding mode. These findings provide converging docking- and dynamics-level evidence that Neoisolongifolene-8-ol is a computationally predicted, structurally stable ligand of pancreatic alpha-amylase. As a purely in silico prediction, this finding does not establish therapeutic efficacy; in vitro kinetic and in vivo validation of this and related E. chlorantha stem bark constituents remain necessary before any candidate can be considered for T2DM management.

item.title: Research Progress and Applications of the Fundamental Principles of Soft Ionization Mass Spectrometry
item.description: (1. Guangdong Huisheng Testing Technology Co., Ltd.) Abstract: Soft ionization mass spectrometry is widely applied in fields such as pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, environmental monitoring, and food safety; however, its fundamental principles remain subject to considerable debate, rendering it a "black-box" technology. This review summarizes the basic principles of electrospray ionization (ESI), matrix-assisted laser desorption (MALDI), and desorption electrospray ionization (DESI), and establishes "one theory, two equations, and three instruments" as the theoretical and practical foundation for soft ionization mass spectrometry. Furthermore, this study discusses the electromagnetic applications of soft ionization mass spectrometry, thereby expanding its scope of research and application.

item.title: Lewis acid-mediated borodegermylation grants access to donor- and acceptor-substituted azaboraspirobifluorenes
item.description: Boron-centered spiro compounds represent a prominent platform for the design of optoelectronic materials. The orthogonally arranged π-conjugated systems around boron enhance stability toward air and moisture, facilitate processing, and allow electronic tuning through donor and acceptor substitution. Synthetic methods reported to date for the preparation of these compounds suffer from low efficiency and poor functional group tolerance, limiting the diversity of accessible electronic materials with tailored properties. Herein, we present a synthetic method leveraging the “Goldilocks” reactivity of germoles among Group 14 analogues to achieve a highly efficient and versatile AlCl3-catalyzed borodegermylation reaction, granting access to donor- and acceptor-functionalized azaboraspirobifluorenes. Furtheremore, the reaction efficiency can be enhanced by employing the sublimed catalyst and the use of an additive. Owing to their high stability, comparatively low toxicity and non-pyrophoric nature, the use of organogermanium compounds provides a more robust and safer alternative to methods that rely on other organometallic reagents.

item.title: Mechanochemically Accelerated Defluorosilylation of α-Trifluoromethyl Styrenes
item.description: We report a mechanochemical copper-catalyzed defluorosilylation of α-trifluoromethyl styrenes with silylboranes. Mechanical activation dramatically accelerated the C–F bond transformation, reducing the reaction time from 8 h to only 30 min at room temperature while substantially decreasing solvent consumption. The reaction exhibits broad substrate compatibility and scalability, highlighting mechanochemistry as an effective strategy for accelerating selective C–F bond functionalization.

item.title: Residue Protonation States Shape the Photodynamics of Red Fluorescent Proteins
item.description: Understanding the protonation equilibria of key residues in fluorescent proteins, particularly those buried and involved in hydrogen bonding with the chromophore, is crucial for modeling their photodynamical behavior. Using mCherry as a model system, we investigate the protonation effects of two ionizable residues, GLU 215 and LYS 70, located within 4 Å of the chromophore, on the protein's photodynamics. Although GLU and LYS should be fully deprotonated and protonated respectively at pH=7.5 and 300K in water, constant pH molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the fractions of protonated GLU 215 and LYS 70 are both near 50% in mCherry at pH=7.5 and 300K. These co-existing protonation microstates modulate chromophore geometry and hydrogen bonding patterns on the ground state, affecting the accessibility of different non-radiative decay pathways on the first singlet excited state (S1). Upon deprotonation of GLU 215 and loss of its hydrogen bond with the chromophore, the protein environment both sterically restricts chromophore twisting and removes the electrostatic driving force for this motion on S1. These findings provide valuable insights for designing brighter red fluorescent proteins by selective stabilization of residue protonation states that block non-radiative decay pathways.

item.title: Supramolecular Eutectogels Based on Mangiferin, a Glucose-Appended Natural Herbal Compound
item.description: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted considerable attention as sustainable, next-generation solvents. In this study, we report the formation of supramolecular eutectogels using mangiferin (MF), a naturally occurring C-glucosyl xanthone. MF successfully induced gelation in typical DESs composed of choline chloride and various hydrogen-bond donors, including urea, ethylene glycol, and glycerol. The gelation behavior was dependent on the hydrogen-bond donor, with significant differences observed in the time required for gelation. Furthermore, microscopic observations and XRD measurements revealed that MF formed distinct self-assembled network structures depending on the DES composition. Rheological measurements revealed the viscoelastic properties of the eutectogels, which supported the formation of three-dimensional supramolecular networks. These findings highlight the potential of MF as a bio-based gelator for DES-based soft materials and provide valuable insights into the rational design of sustainable supramolecular eutectogels for future applications.

item.title: Lithographically Patterned Cobalt Nanoribbons as Magnetic Artificial Pinning Centers in REBCO-Coated Conductors for Continuous-Wave Accelerator Magnets
item.description: We investigate a lithographically patterned cobalt-nanoribbon array as a magnetic artificial pinning center (APC) architecture for REBCO-coated conductors intended for continuous-wave (CW) superconducting accelerator magnets, using accelerator-driven subcritical (ADS) fission-waste-transmutation injectors as the motivating application. A long-wavelength magnetostatic model (the Wallace/Karlqvist spacing-loss approximation used in magnetic-recording physics) is used to estimate the periodic stray-field harmonic produced above the array as a function of the ribbon fill fraction and cobalt-to-REBCO separation and is combined with the standard flux-lattice matching-field relation Bphi = 2*Phi0/(root3 * p^2) to fix the lithographic pitch required for a given target field. This calculation shows that the 13 nm feature size inherited from a prior magic-angle-graphene proposal corresponds to a matching field of approximately 14 T, which is well outside the 0.4–2 T range of published ADS injector solenoid and corrector designs; a pitch of 45–80 nm is required to place the matching field in the ADS-relevant range, and we adopt that corrected target here. This revision replaces the previously illustrated Figure 3 pinning-force bump with a closed-form calculation: the same periodic stray field is combined with the local (Pearl-length) leading-order approximation to the London-theory vortex-ferromagnet interaction energy U_v-Co(x) and force F_v-Co(x) = -dU_v-Co/dx, yielding a nonfitted estimate of the magnetic pinning-force contribution across the 0.4-2 T design range (Section 5.1). That estimate exceeds typical core-pinning energy and cuprate depairing-current scales, which we read as evidence that the local approximation is an upper bound in this regime — expected, since the calculated Pearl length (~45 nm) is comparable to the design pitch — rather than a validated quantitative prediction; the full nonlocal London-theory treatment of the vortex–magnetic-dipole interaction developed by Erdin, Lyuksyutov, Pokrovsky and Vinokur remains the necessary next calculation to convert this upper bound into a quantitative prediction (Section 9). A Rayleigh-law model of minor-loop hysteresis dissipation under near-DC ripple and a toy superposition model of the ribbon orientation-tunable Jc(theta) are presented explicitly as first-order, nonfitted illustrations of the expected functional behavior, not as predictions of specific measured values. The Rayleigh analysis indicates that hysteresis dissipation should be small under strict DC operation but increases as the cube of any residual field ripple, making the power-supply ripple specification a first-order design constraint rather than a negligible detail. No device has been fabricated, and no finite-element or micromagnetic simulation has been performed; together with the full nonlocal London calculation, these remain the specific open questions identified explicitly in Section 9.

item.title: Recycling of PFAS using magnesium through mechanochemical process
item.description: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are widely used a class of organofluorine compounds whose high chemical and thermal stability has motivated the development of strategies for their chemical conversion and fluorine recovery from the perspective of effective fluorine resource utilization. Herein, we report a mechanochemical strategy for the recovery and utilization of fluorine using alkaline-earth metals. Mechanochemical treatment of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) with Mg rapidly converted the fluoropolymer into MgF2, and the method was extended to various PFAS. We further established a method for converting poorly soluble MgF2 into water-soluble NaF by ball milling with NaOH. The poorly water soluble Mg(OH)2 formed during this conversion, which enabled the selective recovery of NaF without additional metal oxide additives. These two transformations were subsequently integrated into a single-step process, enabling the direct conversion of fluoropolymers and perfluoroalkanes into water-soluble and reaildy usable NaF under mechanochemical conditions. The recovered NaF was directly utilized as a fluoride source for one-pot fluorination reactions of sulfonyl chlorides and acyl chlorides, affording the corresponding fluorinated products. This protocol was also scaled up, highlighting important considerations for reaction scale and operational safety. This study provides a useful approach to recovering PFASderived fluorine as a reusable fluoride source and demonstrates its potential for the circular utilization of fluorine resources.

item.title: Methodology for Fabricating and Testing Carbon Molecular Sieve (CMS) Dense Film Membranes for Reproducible Permeation Experiments
item.description: Carbon molecular sieve (CMS) membranes are promising for demanding gas separations, but their brittleness after pyrolysis makes dense-film permeation testing difficult and often irreproducible. Membranes that appear defect-free after pyrolysis can crack during handling, masking, permeation cell assembly, vacuum evacuation or gas pressurization. This work presents a practical procedure for fabricating and testing CMS dense films prepared from fluorinated polyimide-based CMS membranes. We investigated several experimental factors such as polymer concentration, membrane casting in glove bag, epoxy selection, filter paper support, masking and pressure loading, and their resulting impact on the mechanical stability of the membranes Careful control of these steps reduced or entirely mitigated film cracking, gas bypass during testing, and epoxy seal failure during permeation measurements. This study provides a reliable method for casting, masking and testing of fragile CMS dense film membranes and addresses practical details that are often not reported, but are important for successful and reproducible gas permeation data with CMS membranes.

item.title: Photocatalytic dehydrogenation enables divergent access to functional polyolefins
item.description: Polyolefins are among the most widely used plastics, yet their chemically inert hydrocarbon backbones severely limit opportunities for chemical modification and value-added reuse. Introducing carbon–carbon double bonds offers a powerful way to transform these otherwise unreactive materials into versatile intermediates for downstream chemistry. Here we report an acceptorless photocatalytic/cobalt-catalyzed dehydrogenation that operates across a broad range of polyethylene- and polypropylene-based materials, including post-consumer plastics. Notably, polypropylene undergoes dehydrogenation with near-exclusive selectivity for terminal alkene formation. The resulting unsaturated polyolefins serve as versatile platforms for diverse transformations, enabling access to functionalized polyolefins, telechelic polyethylene, as well as block and graft copolymers. These products further demonstrate utility as compatibilizers for immiscible polymer blends and as strong adhesive materials. By converting inert C–H backbones into chemically addressable alkene-containing polymers, this strategy transforms commodity polyolefins into diverse polymer architectures with practical functions.

item.title: Self-Sustained Sabatier Reaction via Submerged Photosynthesis
item.description: CO2 methanation is a promising route for carbon utilization, yet conventional processes remain constrained by their reliance on externally supplied H2 and specialized catalysts. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a self-sustained Sabatier reaction based on the submerged photosynthesis of crystallites (SPSC). In this single aqueous system, metallic Fe and Mg powders react with carbonated water to generate H2 and CH4 near room temperature without an added methanation catalyst. Light irradiation accelerates the production of both gases. CH4 production scales approximately in proportion with H2 generation across diverse reaction conditions, with both gases exhibiting similar apparent activation energies. During the reaction, plate-like FeCO3 forms on the Fe surface, while Mg addition modifies this carbonate structure to enhance relative CH4 formation at longer reaction times. Scavenger experiments confirm the pivotal role of electron transfer in gas production. These results demonstrate that metal oxidation, electron transfer, and surface-bound carbonate reactions drive SPSC-methanation, successfully integrating in situ H2 generation, CH4 formation, and metal carbonate crystallization without external H2 input.

item.title: Sequential Adaptive Natural Density Partitioning (AdNDP) Systematically Produces Non-N-Representable Densities

item.title: Atomic-level visualization of local tacticity and steric structures of polymer chains
item.description: Since Staudinger's demonstration of the macromolecular concept a century ago, polymer science has been built upon the fundamental concept of chain configuration and conformation, which primarily determine polymer properties at both molecular and macroscopic levels. However, direct atomic-level visualization of individual polymer chains has remained a challenge, leaving the fundamental question of how local chain configuration/conformation are involved in the preferred overall chain morphology experimentally unexplored. Here, we present a novel approach combining atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy, molecular mechanics simulation, and a genetic algorithm to determine the atomic-level structures of single polymer chains. This hybrid experimental-computational method successfully visualizes both the local stereochemical configuration, i.e., tacticity, and backbone conformations (dihedral angles) of a single chain adsorbed on a substrate at the atomic level. Significantly, we demonstrate experimentally that chain shapes result from a balance between intrinsic local conformational energy, influenced by local tacticity, and extrinsic environmental factors, including substrate adsorption energy and surface geometric constraints. Our approach extends fundamental experimental insights into single-chain physics, enabling the rational design of polymeric materials with more precisely controlled molecular architectures.

item.title: MaRs: A Universal Python Library for Steady-State and Time-Resolved EPR Simulations
item.description: MaRs is an open-source Python library for the simulation and fitting of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra. MaRs supports simulations of field-swept and frequency-swept continuous-wave EPR, accounting for various spin-sublevel polarizations. Moreover, MaRs is capable of simulating complete 2D time-resolved EPR spectra (in field-time domain). The latter can be computed in different levels of theoretical complexity. First, the time evolution can be computed either with kinetic rate equations, which describe population transfer, or in full Liouville space, which captures coherence dynamics. Second, the relaxation pathways in timeresolved simulations can be specified either through intuitive rate parameters that are automatically expanded into the Lindblad master-equation form, or derived microscopically using the Bloch-Redfield formalism. To handle physically complex relaxation scenarios, MaRs provides automatic thermal-balance enforcement and composition operations that allow multicomponent relaxation models to be assembled from simple building blocks. Built on PyTorch (popular platform for machine learning development), MaRs leverages operations on both CPU and CUDA (GPU) backends. We demonstrate MaRs time-resolved EPR capabilities as well the differences and limitations of each built-in approach to time-domain simulations on the examples of coupled triplet-doublet pairs and systems exhibiting the reverse intersystem crossing phenomenon. Separately, we validate stationary EPR simulations across diverse spin systems, including high-spin complexes, achieving excellent agreement with established packages. We also show the possibilities of parameter fitting framework, applicable to all spectrum types implemented in MaRs, that supports multiple optimization strategies and uncertainty quantification.

item.title: Imitation and Accuracy in Automated Electronic-Structure Method Selection
Volatile-element depletion in rocky planets as a purity spectrum of a single information field: An information-dynamics reinterpretation of hybrid accretion
item.description: Wang et al. (2026, Nature Astronomy) showed that the moderately-volatile lithophile element (MVLE) depletion patterns of Earth and Mars record different formation pathways: Earth accreted ≳75% of its mass via pebble accretion, Mars ∼73% via collisions of volatile-depleted planetesimals. We reinterpret this result in the information-dynamics (ID) framework, in which self-organization (ε) and dissipation (γ) compete through a single information field of local purity p. A numerical experiment on the published source data (13 elements for bulk silicate Earth, bulk silicate Mars and Vesta) shows that a single mean purity cannot describe the two planets: the fit escapes to unphysical solutions. The data instead require a purity spectrum: each planet’s pattern is a mixture over one universal single-purity response law S(T ; p), with only the mixture weights differing between bodies. A joint fit with a 4-parameter universal law reproduces all 36 data points with χ2/N = 0.35 (all residuals within 2σ). The inferred spectra mirror the published multi-component decomposition (Earth: 59% strongly-processed + 24% Vesta-like + 17% volatile-rich; Mars: Vesta-like bin dominant), and Vesta independently concentrates 99% of its weight at a processing temperature of 1116K, reproducing the published 1135±35K without being given it. Pebble accretion and planetesimal collision thus emerge as two projections of the same field at different purities, rather than two independent mechanisms. We give testable predictions for rocky exoplanets and the Moon.

item.title: Dry-drawn Bi2Te3-on-paper thermoresistive devices for respiration monitoring
item.description: Dry deposition on paper offers a simple route to resistive sensing devices. Here, micronized Bi2Te3 powder is rubbed onto copier paper through a tape mask, charcoal electrodes are drawn over the deposited layer, and copper leads are attached with conductive silver paste; the active layer requires no solvent, binder, vacuum processing or annealing. X-ray diffraction identifies rhombohedral Bi2Te3 with preferred (00l) orientation, while electron microscopy shows particles and platelets distributed over the fibrous substrate. Between 25 and 60 °C, the resistance of three devices follows an Arrhenius relationship with an apparent activation energy of 0.121 ± 0.005 eV, corresponding to a temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) of −1.6 % °C−1 at 25 °C, several times larger in magnitude than that of pencil-drawn graphite. A room-temperature air puff onto a device held at 40 °C produces a 10–90 % response within ≈0.2 s, limited by the sampling rate of 10 readings s−1. Covering the channel with adhesive tape reduces the resistance change between 30 and 90 % relative humidity from ≈−30 % to less than 1 %. In a self-experiment by one of the authors, a tape-covered device positioned ≈1 cm below the nostrils exhibits resistance modulations of 2.3–7.2 % during bilateral and single-nostril breathing, with dominant spectral frequencies of 22–23 min−1. These results establish dry-drawn Bi2Te3 as a simple, solvent-free thermoresistive sensing material on paper and demonstrate its feasibility for respiration monitoring.

item.title: Hybrid Photoactive Lignin Based Magnetic Nanomaterials for Antimicrobial Application
A Broadly Deployable Method for Repeated Hyperpolarized 13C Metabolic Imaging in Living Animals
item.description: Hyperpolarized 13C-MRI enables real-time imaging of metabolic conversions in vivo, but remains largely restricted to specialized sites with superconducting high-field MRI and polarization infrastructure. Here we present a broadly deployable method for preclinical hyperpolarized 13C-metabolic imaging, which combines signal amplification by reversible exchange (SABRE), a parahydrogen-based hyperpolarization technique, with detection of [1-13C]pyruvate-d3 in a compact 436 mT permanent-magnet small-animal MRI system. SABRE yields 13C-pyruvate polarization of 13% at ~30 mM in a purified, biocompatible solution, with a T1 relaxation time of 140 s. In a transgenic breast cancer mouse model, 13C-chemical shift imaging after injection resolves pyruvate, pyruvate hydrate and lactate in vivo, maps elevated lactate-to-pyruvate ratios in mammary tumors and images three freshly prepared pyruvate doses sequentially in the same animal in less than one hour. This compact SABRE-to-low-field method makes repeated hyperpolarized 13C-metabolic imaging mobile and accessible in standard preclinical research environments.

item.title: Direct Photo- and Electrothermally Regenerable Adsorbents for Carbon Dioxide Capture Using Conjugated Metal−Organic Frameworks
item.description: Adsorbent regeneration in carbon dioxide capture systems primarily relies on external temperature and pressure swings, posing critical challenges of intensive energy penalties and low cycling rates. Here we demonstrate a direct photo- and electrothermal swing method for CO2 capture using two-dimensional conjugated MOF Cu3(2,3,6,7,10,11-hexahydroxytriphenylene)2 (Cu3(HHTP)2) and its derivatives. Cu3(HHTP)2 releases CO2 captured at room-temperature through photo- or electrothermal effects by directly applying one-sun irradiation or a voltage of 10 V. The capture-release process operates across 1%-50% CO2 with a cyclic frequency of 4-5 h-1 and adsorption capacities of 0.04-1.11 mmol g-1. Incorporating alkylamine groups into Cu3(HHTP)2 further enhances CO2 adsorption capacity by more than three-fold, with corresponding energy consumptions down to 145 and 60 kJ mol-1 for 1% and 10% CO2, respectively, via photothermal regeneration. Structurally integrating energy conversion functions and CO2 adsorption sites within a single, porous material establishes a new blueprint for solar-driven and electrified carbon management.

item.title: Nonadiabatic Semiclassical Polariton Dynamics: Excited State Proton Transfer of Aminopropenal
item.description: The interplay between strong light-matter coupling and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics provides a promising route to control chemical reactivity. Here, we develop a framework for simulating polaritonic chemistry with on-the-fly semiclassical nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, employing the linearized semiclassical initial value representation. With this approach, we simulate the nonadiabatic molecular dynamics under strong light-matter coupling, presenting results for excited state proton transfer of aminopropenal. Light-matter interactions are described using a Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian formulated in the adiabatic electronic basis, where the electronic energies, transition moments, and nuclear forces are evaluated on the fly. We characterize how light-matter coupling reshapes reaction pathways and redistributes photonic and electronic character of individual states along the trajectory, finding that photonic character of the lower polaritonic state decreases in time as the molecular geometry relaxes, demonstrating that the cavity effect is strongest during the initial dynamics. We find that for aminopropenal, the main effect of cavity coupling on the dynamics is not altering the proton transfer barrier, but instead altering the excited-state relaxation network by introducing an additional polaritonic state with favorable proton transfer energetics. By analyzing the population transfer between excited states, we find that cavity coupling leads to population being temporarily redirected into this intermediate state, delaying population relaxation to a high-barrier excited state. This change in timing results in a higher fraction of trajectories undergoing proton transfer. Our new computational protocol that connects on-the-fly semiclassical nonadiabatic dynamics and polaritonic frameworks provides trajectory-resolved insight into how cavity coupling modifies nonadiabatic population transfer and proton-transfer dynamics.

item.title: Mayer’s Effective Minimal Localized Molecular Orbitals
item.description: Roughly thirty years ago Mayer presented a theory leading to the concept of an effective minimal atomic basis. A set of a posteriori defined, fragment-localized molecular orbitals (LMOs) was obtained as a byproduct. In this work, a new set of LMOs, termed Mayer’s effective minimal LMOs, is derived from this byproduct; it can be viewed as arising from a compactification of atomic orbitals projected onto the occupied space. The procedure is fully self-contained, requiring no input beyond that of the underlying quantum chemical calculation. The resulting LMOs are orientation invariant, computationally economical, and can be partitioned into disjoint subsets assigned to atoms or multiatomic fragments. Mayer’s effective minimal LMOs span the occupied space, but their number exceeds its dimension; they therefore form a frame rather than a basis in the strict sense. The size of the set does not grow with the original AO basis but remains at a value prescribed by the user, a prudent choice being the minimal atomic orbital basis dimension.

item.title: From Promotion to Poisoning: Temperature- and Coverage-Dependent Effects of Trace Fe on the Hydrogen Evolution Activity of Pt
item.description: Trace iron impurities can strongly alter the alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), yet how temperature governs their surface accumulation and kinetic consequences remains poorly understood. Here, the influence of 0–60 ppb Fe impurities on polycrystalline Pt was systematically examined in 0.1 M KOH over 280–336 K. Fe addition progressively suppressed the hydrogen underpotential-deposition (Hupd) charge, indicating blockage of Pt sites by Fe-derived surface species, while this suppression was substantially mitigated at elevated temperature. Despite this site blocking, 10–20 ppb Fe enhanced the HER current, whereas further Fe addition caused pronounced deactivation, particularly at 280–298 K. Wide-potential-range voltammetry revealed electrochemical responses consistent with hydroxide-like Fe species undergoing an Fe(II)/Fe(III)-type redox transition, with the Fe-associated anodic charge decreasing markedly at 336 K. Apparent thermodynamic analyses further indicated that Fe-induced site blocking cannot be described by adsorption on a single population of independent, equivalent sites. Most importantly, correlation of the Hupd-derived blocked-site fraction with the Tafel slope revealed three coverage-dependent regimes: kinetic promotion at low Fe coverage, predominantly site-number-limited deactivation at intermediate coverage, and severe kinetic inhibition at high coverage. These results demonstrate that trace Fe does not behave as a simple inert poison but dynamically modifies the Pt/Fe-derived interface in a coverage- and temperature-dependent manner. The findings establish electrolyte temperature and trace-impurity coverage as coupled parameters controlling alkaline HER kinetics on Pt.

item.title: Heteroatom Engineering Enables Oxygen-Tolerant Electrochemical Direct Air Capture
item.description: Electrochemical direct CO2 capture using redox-active carriers offers an alternative to thermal amine scrubbing but requires molecules that combine strong CO2 binding with tolerance toward oxygen and water. Here, we show that incorporating pyridinic nitrogen into an ortho-quinone framework provides this combination in 1,10phenanthroline-5,6-dione (PD). Comparison of PD with phenanthrenequinone (PQ) and the analogue 1,10phenanthroline (PT) isolates the role of pyridinic nitrogen in tuning the redox potential and CO2 capture behaviour of the quinone core. Electrochemical measurements, density functional theory (DFT), in situ FT-IR, and 13C NMR spectroscopy support strong and reversible CO2 binding through the electrochemically reduced dianion (log𝐾 = 9.8). The capture chemistry established in homogeneous electrolyte was subsequently translated to PD immobilised on a carbon-felt electrode and demonstrated in a near-neutral aqueous electrolyte. Under a 9.3% CO2 feed, the PD-modified electrode sustained reversible CO2 capture and release over 16 h with an electron-utilisation efficiency of 96% and a minimum energy requirement of 44-56 kJ mol-1 CO2. Isotope-sensitive in situ FT-IR measurements and the pH response during aqueous cycling further support cation participation in charge compensation. These results establish heteroatom engineering as a molecular design strategy for developing oxygen- and water-tolerant quinone redox carriers and provide a pathway toward electrochemical CO2 capture from dilute emission streams.

item.title: Aryne-Enabled Synthesis of 1,8-Disubstituted Thioxanthones for Conformationally Gated Metal-Ion Sensing
item.description: Conformational changes in a chromophore can strongly influence its fluorescence properties. Here, we report the development of thioxanthone-based fluorescent sensors designed to suppress the characteristic butterfly-like deformation of the thioxanthone core upon metal-ion binding. To access the required 1,8-disubstituted scaffolds, we developed an efficient aryne-based synthesis of multisubstituted thioxanthones from readily available o-iodoaryl triflates and N,N,N’,N’-tetramethylthiourea. Subsequent functionalization provided a series of thioxanthones bearing metal-coordinating substituents at the 1,8-positions. Evaluation of the resulting compounds identified a probe exhibiting pronounced and spectrally distinct fluorescence responses to Zn2+ and Ca2+ with high ON/OFF ratios, enabling clear discrimination between the two metal ions. Time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations for a simplified Zn2+ complex indicated that coordination stabilizes a nearly planar thioxanthone structure and enhances the oscillator strength of the emissive transition. These results demonstrate the utility of controlling the butterfly-like deformation of the thioxanthone core for metal-ion-responsive fluorescence sensing.

item.title: Synthesis of Amphiphilic Polymer Co-Networks via the Growth of a Living RAFT Network. Part III: Effect of DMSO Content
item.description: Owing to their distinctive nanophase-separated, co-continuous morphology, Amphiphilic polymer co-networks (APCNs) have attracted considerable attention in the past four decades. In 2024, a RAFT-mediated network growth strategy for the synthesis of APCNs was reported. This approach involves first preparing a parent RAFT network, typically a hydrophilic network containing dormant network-RAFT agents, followed by the diffusion and polymerization of hydrophobic monomers within the parent network. This process generates a secondary hydrophobic nanophase within the pre-existing hydrophilic continuous phase, yielding an amphiphilic polymer co-network that fulfils the defining structural characteristics of APCNs. This work reports a systematic study of the effect of DMSO content (10%, 50%, and 75%) on the synthesis of amphiphilic polymer co-networks (APCNs) using the above-mentioned RAFT-mediated network growth strategy. The resulting APCNs comprise a hydrophilic parent network based on oligo(ethylene glycol) methyl ether acrylate (OEGA, Mn = 480) and the crosslinker N, N′-methylenebisacrylamide (Bis), into which hydrophobic n-butyl acrylate (BA) segments are incorporated through RAFT-mediated network growth. Network chemical composition, thermal properties, and morphology were characterized using FT-IR, TGA, DSC, and SEM, while amphiphilicity was assessed through equilibrium swelling measurements in water and toluene. The DMSO content employed during parent network synthesis was found to exert a pronounced effect on the properties of the resulting APCNs. Among the systems investigated, the APCN derived from a parent gel prepared in 75% DMSO and subjected to 5 h of photogrowth exhibited the most balanced amphiphilic character, displaying swelling ratios of 10.30 in water and 18.24 in toluene.

item.title: Scalable Synthesis and Processing of Porous Organic Polymers for Continuous-Flow Noble Metal Recycling and Catalysis
item.description: Porous organic polymers (POPs) hold great promise for separations and catalysis but remain limited by costly syntheses and poor processability. Here we report the scalable synthesis of freestanding imine/aminal-linked POP gels from inexpensive monomers under mild conditions. The gels can be molded into diverse architectures and converted into mechanically robust monoliths with high surface areas of up to 1055 m2/g. The POPs exhibit high adsorption capacities of 3225 mg/g for [AuCl4]- and 1375 mg/g for [PdCl4]2-. Integrated into continuousflow columns, they enable the treatment of electronic-waste leachates at a throughput of 1 L/h, achieving a gold recovery efficiency of 99%. The noble-metal-loaded POP column can be operated as a continuous-flow Suzuki reactor, delivering a space–time yield of 2.75 kgbiphenyl/LPOP·day. This work establishes a practical platform for fabrication of scalable, processable POPs that integrate noble-metal recovery with continuous-flow catalysis, advancing their application toward circular resource utilization and sustainable chemical manufacturing.

item.title: Probing the Softer-acid Nature of 102No2+ Compared to Alkaline Earth Metal ions via Synergistic Extraction with Sulfur Donor on Crown Ether Supported Resin
item.description: Unlike other f block elements that typically exhibit +3 or higher oxidation states, nobelium (No, atomic number = 102) exists predominantly as the divalent cation in aqueous solutions. While No2+ has long been considered chemically analogous to Ca2+ and Sr2+, strong relativistic effects are predicted to alter its reactivity. In our previous study, the soft metal ion behavior of No2+ was demonstrated through complexation with crown ethers. Prompted by this implication, in this study, we performed online solid-liquid extraction experiments of 255No by employing diethyl dithiophosphate (DEDTP−) as a soft sulfur-donor ligand to probe the softer Lewis acid character of No relative to alkaline earth metals via No–S bonding. Here we report the results of the experiments and relativistic DFT calculations. In the Sr resin/HDEDTP (aqueous) system, No2+ behaves in a manner distinct from Ca2+ and Sr2+, resembling Ba2+ and Ra2+. No2+ exhibits a significantly higher extraction efficiency in the HDEDTP system than Sr2+, confirming enhanced soft Lewis acid character. The computed Gibbs free energies of extraction-complex formation are consistent with the experimental ΔG trend, validating the theoretical model. The optimized geometry revealed a No–S bond shorter than ionic radius trends, indicating stronger bonding. We attribute this distinctive behavior to unique electronic states of No. Specifically, higher electron gain in the d-orbital, stronger relativistic 7s stabilization, and closer 5f energy matching synergistically enhance covalent character of No–S bonding.

item.title: Fe-dopant site occupancy in Co3O4: evidence of isovalent substitution and short-range association at octahedral sites
item.description: Understanding how dopant site occupancy influences the behavior of spinel oxides is essential for tailoring their functional properties. Here, we combine DFT+U calculations with computational and experimental Co K-edge XANES spectroscopy to investigate the structural, electronic, and magnetic effects of Fe incorporation into Co3O4. The results indicate a strong energetic preference for isovalent substitution, with Fe3+ preferentially occupying octahedral Co3+ sites. This preference becomes more pronounced with increasing dopant concentration, leading to a clear stability hierarchy in which short-distance double-octahedral configurations are energetically favored. Dopant–dopant interactions further influence this stability landscape, promoting attractive coupling for octahedral and mixed-site configurations, while tetrahedral Fe3+ exhibits weak or slightly repulsive interactions. These trends are reflected in the magnetic properties, with octahedral Fe inducing stronger local magnetic moments compared to tetrahedral substitution. The calculated XANES spectra reveal site-dependent modifications of the Co pre-edge features that can be related to changes in the local electronic structure induced by Fe doping. However, these spectral changes should be interpreted qualitatively in light of known limitations of the theoretical approach. Overall, this study highlights the central role of dopant site occupancy, in addition to dopant concentration, in tuning the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of Co3O4 spinels.

item.title: Microstructural, Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy, and Fourier-Transform Infrared Analysis of Inorganic-Platelet Polymer Composites for Sustainable Infrastructure
item.description: Polymer matrix composites used in wet or thermally variable environments may change through moisture diffusion, polymer relaxation, swelling and plasticization, hydrolysis or leaching, microcracking, and progressive weakening of the reinforcement–matrix interface. This paper focuses on understanding the composition and morphology of a reinforcing phase, and determining whether its incorporation produces additional bulk-resolvable chemical features, which is important for interpreting composites used in wet or aggressive environments. The study presents a structural and spectroscopic characterization of a commercial glass-flake-reinforced unsaturated-polyester composite by combining energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) with full-range Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) against a neat unsaturated-polyester-resin control. EDS gives a composition consistent with a sodium–calcium silicate glass phase for the flake (17.4 wt% Si, 5.0 wt% Na, 2.2 wt% Ca, 1.1 wt% Al, 1.0 wt% Mg and 55.6 wt% O), whereas the polyester matrix and coat regions are dominated by carbon and oxygen (70–75 wt% C and 23–26 wt% O). Two representative flakes (n = 2) have apparent length-to-width ratios of 21.9 and 43.9. FTIR spectra collected over 428–4500 cm-1 show the same principal polyester-resin-associated bands at essentially identical wavenumbers in the composite and neat resin. Polymer-associated band intensities are 12–28% lower in the composite, while the band near the Si–O–Si network bending region changes by only −0.6%. No additional resolvable bulk absorption bands are observed. The results support a physically dispersed silicate-glass phase within the polyester matrix but do not exclude weak or spatially localized interfacial interactions below the resolution of the measurements. The spectra and elemental tables are released as a reusable dataset.

item.title: Stable triorganoiodine complexes
item.description: The first examples of air stable acyclic triorganoiodine compounds, phenyliodine bis(1-(2-R)-o-carborane)s have been isolated from reactions of PhIL2 reagents with lithio-o-carboranes and crystallographically characterized. When R = H or Si(CH3)3, the complexes are predisposed to form o-carboryne through β-elimination as confirmed by a trapping reaction with naphthalene, where the R = H variant degrades during formation. The latter Si(CH3)3 derivative is isolable in modest yield, while for R = CH3, the resulting phenyliodine bis(1-(2-methyl)-o-carborane)s can be obtained in high yields. The complexes known so far appear to behave as nonnucleophilic bases, and treatment with strong protic acids affords more electrophilic phenyl(1-o-carboranyl) iodonium salts. Compared with our previous synthesis of an aryl(1-o-carboranyl) iodonium salt, this method is simpler and offers broadened scope. Less is known of these salts than previously assumed as earlier reports have now also been found incorrect. A preliminary study finds they can either arylate or 1-o-carboranylate a chloride nucleophile with chemoselectivity tuneable by electronic modification of the oCb ligand, providing a rare example of an o-carborane C atom reacting as an electrophile.

item.title: Predicting Glass Transition Temperature of Polyimide Homopolymers and Copolymers Using Interpretable QSPR-Based Machine Learning: The MFKit Framework
item.description: In this work, we address the problem of predicting the glass transition temperature of polyimides, a class of high-performance engineering thermoplastics, with an emphasis on both homopolymer and copolymer systems. While machine learning approaches have been widely applied to polymer property prediction, their extension to copolymers remains limited and often lacks the interpretability required for rational materials design. To overcome these limitations, we develop an interpretable QSPR-based framework (MFKit) that combines physically grounded descriptors for monomer featurization with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). The model is trained on a dataset of polyimide homopolymers from PoLyInfo and achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches (R2 = 0.856, MAE = 20.7 °C on the test set). Causal inference and SHAP analysis reveal key structure–property relationships, identifying aromatic content, backbone flexibility and rotation, side chain volume and hydrogen bonding as dominant factors governing Tg. The framework is subsequently extended to polyimide copolymers by constructing copolymer representations through combination of monomer descriptor vectors using several aggregation schemes. The best-performing approach yields R2 = 0.832 and MAE = 23.3 °C on an external dataset compiled from the literature. Furthermore, guided by the identified structure–property relationships, polyimide copolymers are designed, synthesized, and experimentally characterized, each exhibiting increased Tg compared with the parent homopolymer. Validation against DSC measurements demonstrates strong agreement with predictions (MAE = 16.3 °C). Overall, the proposed approach provides a unified and interpretable framework for Tg prediction for both homopolymer and copolymer systems, enabling physically grounded and data-driven design of polyimide-based materials.

item.title: De novo design of photoenzymes with substrate-recognition-encoded enantioselectivity
item.description: Photoenzymes enable stereoselective excited-state transformations beyond the chemical space accessible to natural enzymes, yet their development remains largely dependent on repurposing few privileged protein scaffolds and extensive directed evolution. Although de novo protein design enables tailor-made catalytic architectures, its prevailing transition-state stabilization paradigm is not readily transferable to photoenzymes. Here we establish a substrate-recognition-guided strategy for de novo photoenzyme design, in which the computational construction of substrate-tailored catalytic environments determines stereoselectivity and the genetic incorporation of abiotic thioxanthone photosensitizer endows excited-state reactivity. This approach generated customized photoenzymes for the deracemization of 4-alkenylcyclohexanols that exhibit nanomolar substrate affinity, catalytic efficiencies exceeding 1.5 × 105 M-1 s-1, and up to 99% enantiomeric excess. Crystal structure and kinetic analyses validate the designed model, revealing substrate-recognition-dependent enantioselective energy transfer within the tailored active site. This work establishes substrate recognition as a general design principle for extending de novo enzyme design to excited-state biocatalysis.

item.title: Terminal Acceptor-Substitution Controls Optoelectronic Properties in Triphenylamine Based Donors for Organic Solar Cells: A DFT Approach
item.description: Organic solar cells offer opportunities for lightweight and flexible solar energy conversion, motivating development of molecular systems with tunable optoelectronic properties. In this study, six novel triphenylamine-based small-molecule donors (RD1-RD6) having donor-πacceptor (D-π-A) design, where dimethoxy triphenylamine-donor, thiophene-bridge, and phenyl with 1,3-indandione derivatives-acceptors are investigated to understand how the terminal acceptor regulates their molecular, electronic and excited state properties. Density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations are employed to understand their structural, optoelectronic and charge-transfer properties. Terminal acceptors via different substitutions systematically modulate frontier orbital energies, with HOMO-LUMO gaps ranging from 1.62 to 2.23 eV, absorption maxima of 396-469 nm, and pronounced intramolecular charge transfer characteristics reaching 69.57%. RD6 exhibited the deepest HOMO (-4.96 eV), highest calculated dipole moment (21.33 D) in methanol, and substantial electron-hole separation, whereas RD3 exhibited the narrowest HOMO-LUMO gap (1.62 eV). All the molecules showed low reorganization energies especially for electrons (0.02 - 0.08 eV), high light-harvesting efficiencies (0.89 - 0.98), and favorable intrinsic charge-transfer characteristics. A Scharber-type model applied to RD6 predicts theoretical PCEs of 18.50% and 19.83% for the binary RD6:Y6-2Cl and ternary RD6:L8-BO:Y6-2Cl configuration. Overall, the results demonstrate that terminal acceptor engineering provides an effective way for tuning electronic and excited-state properties of triphenylamine-based donors.

item.title: De Novo Circularly Polarized Emission and Greatly Enhanced Circular Dichroism in Cationic Naphthalene Diimide Dye Supramolecular Assembly on 2-D Laponite Nanoclay
item.description: This study reveals a surprising finding that a chiral cationic pyrrolidine-substituted naphthalene diimide (cNDI-Py+), which shows no circular dichroism (CD) or circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) in its monomeric form, exhibits strong CD and broad, intense CPL when electrostatically bound to a 2D synthetic laponite nanoclay nanoplatelet (cNDI-Py+_Laponite) in an aqueous environment. This supramolecular alignment of the electrostatically anchored dye on laponite platelets leads to a chiral assembly that produces distinctive chiral excimer emission, stemming from an excited-state slip-stacked arrangement of preorganized dye molecules. The new hybrid emission band at 480 nm comes from the excited cNDI-Py+_Laponite assembly, as evidenced by a high quantum yield (Φ) of 0.40, luminescence dissymmetry (glum) of -0.013, and an outstanding CPL brightness of 88 M-1 cm-1. We demonstrate that chiral dye-nanoclay assemblies serve as an underused platform for excimer-based CPL by nanoscale confinement of dye molecules. Bright circularly polarized emissions can play an important role in establishing experimental space-to-ground telecommunication links, enabling full-color 3D holographic displays, and supporting other applications that rely on chiral control of light-matter interactions. This approach provides oxygen-tolerant control with inorganic templates, enabling enantioselective excimer emission and opening new paths for CPL-active materials.

item.title: Enantioselective [3+3] Formal Annulation of Anilines via Carbene Catalysis
item.description: An efficient preparation of highly enantioenriched cyclic compounds from readily available synthons via stereocontrolled organocatalytic processes remains a significant challenge in modern synthetic chemistry. Herein, we report a highly stereoselective N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed [3+3] annulation of anilines using α-bromocinnamic aldehydes as convenient acyl-azolium precursors. This protocol offers a straightforward route to valuable chiral lactams in high yields (up to 98%) and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 97:3 er), featuring broad functional group tolerance. Moreover, the reaction is easily scalable and enables versatile downstream derivatizations, further demonstrating the synthetic utility of the developed methodology.

item.title: Robust and Reusable Waveguide-Enhanced Raman-on-a-Chip for Sensing Complex Fluids
item.description: Integrated photonic sensors offer a pathway toward compact chemical analysis, but their use in unprocessed complex fluids is limited by surface fouling, chemical compatibility, and the need for stable optical coupling. Here, we develop a reusable waveguide-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (WERS) platform based on chemically resilient silicon nitride waveguides and a permanently packaged fiber-to-chip interface. The sensor incorporates a spiral sensing waveguide and a robust optical input/output architecture designed to provide reproducible coupling without active alignment. Reusability was evaluated following exposure to commercial gasoline and sequential cleaning treatments. Raman signal recovery using isopropanol as a reference analyte demonstrated improved spectral performance after solvent and oxidative cleaning. As a representative application in a chemically complex matrix, the sensor was directly immersed in commercial gasoline for quantitative ethanol determination without extraction or additional sample preparation. A ratiometric signal based on the ethanol band at 885 cm-1 and a reference band at 1000 cm-1 provided a linear calibration over 10.00–21.74% v/v ethanol (R2 = 0.9323). Independent external validation across 10.00–20.00% v/v yielded 100% prediction-interval coverage, an RMSEP of 0.46% v/v, and an MAE of 0.36% v/v. These results demonstrate that chemically robust WERS with stable packaging can support reproducible, reusable Raman sensing directly in complex fuel matrices, providing a foundation for field-deployable photonic chemical analysis.

item.title: Quantum-Entangled Four-Proton Waltz of Anomalous Transport in Water Hydrogen Bond Network
item.description: Proton transfer mechanism along water hydrogen bond network lies in the fundamental question in chemical dynamics. The mechanism remains challenge due to nuclear quantization and many-body correlation. We develop a quantum dynamical model framework that treats electrons and multiple transferring protons on equal footing, and integrate it with isotope measurement by scanning tunneling microscopy of a surface‑bound water tetramer. The simulations reveal the importance of quantum correlation among stepwise electron–proton intermediate states, which quantum coherently drives a synchronized, concerted four‑proton switch between two chiral hydrogen‑bond configurations. Populations periodically decay from one chiral arrangement and reappear in the other, whose oscillation amplitude is strongly suppressed by modest symmetry breaking from isotopic substitution. This mechanism accounts for an anomalous isotope trend experimentally in which the low‑symmetry, singly deuterated tetramer (H2O)3(D2O) switches as slowly as the high‑symmetry, fully deuterated (D2O)4 that eludes semiclassical tunneling kinetics. The framework establishes a practical route to study multi-proton quantum correlation in hydrogen-bond networks on surfaces.

item.title: One-step synthesis of α-fluoroarylacetic acids from trifluoromethyl arenes via photocatalytic reduction
item.description: A photocatalytic reduction strategy for the direct synthesis of α-fluoroarylacetic acids from readily available trifluoromethyl arenes has been developed. In contrast to conventional approaches, this reaction does not generate undesired oxidation byproducts associated with the use of fluorinating reagents. Investigation of the substrate scope revealed that the reaction tolerates a wide range of functional groups, including dimethylamino, alkynyl, alkenyl, and ether functionalities. Trifluoromethyl-substituted pyridine derivatives were also compatible with the reaction conditions. Mechanistic studies suggested that the reaction proceeds via an initial hydrodefluorination to form a difluoromethyl arene intermediate, followed by further reductive C–F bond cleavage and carboxylation. The observed selectivity for the monofluorinated products originated from the selective carboxylation during product formation together with the slow hydrodefluorination of the resulting α-fluoroarylacetic acids. The reaction proceeds without the need for an external CO2 atmosphere.

item.title: Graph Theory-Based De Novo Strategy for Automated Generation of Organic Molecular Cage
item.description: The current design and construction of organic molecular cages (OMCs) remain largely constrained by established topological library. To address this challenge, we established a de novo, graph-theory-based strategy that enables the automated generation of OMCs architectures, which require only the chemical structures of building blocks. By decomposing OMCs into distinct topological geometric elements, a system of equations can be established using graph theory to describe the mathematical relationships and geometric constraints for their architectures. Solving these equations yields the numerical composition of the topological geometric elements for each candidate OMC, allowing the potential rotational symmetries of their architectures to be inferred. Based on the inferred rotational symmetries, a database of OMC topologies was systematically established by applying symmetry operations to define the connectivity between geometric elements. Subsequently, different molecular building blocks were incorporated into these topologies, followed by geometry optimization to generate a large space of chemically realistic three-dimensional OMC structures. This strategy enabled the generation of OMCs with previously unexplored topologies, substantially expanding the structural diversity of the OMCs’ chemical space. To further enrich this chemical space, we extended our strategy to encompass isomers arising from mixed or prochiral building blocks. This strategy enables the systematic exploration of previously overlooked OMC topologies and their corresponding isomers, providing a foundation for the targeted design of molecular cages with tailored cavity geometries, pore sizes, and chemical environments for applications in molecular recognition, selective separation and catalysis.

item.title: Transition state to minimum conversion in the Cope rearrangement under gigapascal pressure
item.description: Converting a transition state (TS) into a minimum is a challenging, yet possible, task, commonly achievable via chemical substitution. Pressure is expected to favor TSs that correspond to volume minima, yet experimentally or computationally demonstrated TS-to-minimum conversions remain rare. Here, we demonstrate a pressure-induced TS-to-minimum conversion in the Cope rearrangement at ∼18 GPa. Extreme pressure polarizable continuum model (XP-PCM) optimizations and vibrational analyses reveal the gradual conversion of the TS imaginary mode into a real vibrational mode. Helium compression chamber (HeCC) simulations unveil a pressure-driven inversion of the reaction-path curvature at the TS in the Gibbs free energy profile. Cyano substitution produces effects on bond distances and vibrational frequencies similar to those induced by pressure, highlighting parallels between chemical and mechanical stabilization. Although compression also accelarates the open-shell pathway, the closed-shell pathway remains thermodynamically favored up to 31 GPa. These findings highlight pressure as a powerful means of reshaping reaction landscapes, effectively enabling new chemistry.

item.title: Investigation of NaxFePO4 systems prepared by a modified Pechini sol-gel method as possible cathode materials for high voltage Na-ion batteries
item.description: An uncomplicated modification of a Pechini assisted sol-gel process in water-polyol solutions is proposed for the synthesis of Na-Fe phosphate powders with different Na-ion content as cathode materials for sodium ion batteries (SIBs). Depending on the pH-values, X-ray diffraction detected the formation of Na-poor olivine-like o-NaFePO4 orthorhombic phase and o-FePO4 nanocrystalline structure. The cyclic voltammetry of the SIBs shows reduction peaks at ~2.23 V (x = 1.0) and ~2.12 V (x = 1.2) vs. Na/Na+ for pH < 3, and between 2.8 V - ~3.0 V (x = 1.0) for pH = 5 respectively. For x = 1.2, several redox peaks observed for pH=5 are assigned to a single-phase reaction (at ~2.5 V vs. Na/Na+) and two-phase reactions (at 3.0–3.25 V). Redox peaks above 4.5 V are more likely associated with Fe3+/Fe4+ redox coupling. A good cyclability is observed for the cathodes synthesized at both the pH values even by charging the batteries to the upper cut-off 4.8 V. The Na-cathode materials prepared under milder conditions showed the highest specific capacity of 40 mAhg-1.

item.title: Polymorphism and Dimensionality in Rhodium Chalcogenide Nanocrystals
item.description: Rhodium chalcogenides have rich crystal chemistry and offer opportunities in catalytic chemical transformations, quantum phenomena and devices, and biological applications. However, their solution phase chemistry, particularly the synthesis of specific phases with well-defined dimensionality, remains nascent. Here, we report a colloidal strategy to access multiple air-stable 5-30 nm nanocrystals of binary rhodium chalcogenides, including Rh0.78Se (P63/mmc), 2D (Pm1) RhTe2, 3D (Pa) RhTe2, and Rh3Te8 (R). We demonstrate how the choices of precursors and injection (Tinj) and growth temperatures (Tgrowth) enable their phase selective synthesis. Analyses by powder X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy verify the compositions and phase purities of the different nanocrystalline samples. Density functional theory calculations confirm metallic character of the binary rhodium chalcogenides and unveil the relative stabilities of different RhCh2 polymorphs (Ch = Se, Te). For example, we find that the synthesized trigonal 2D (Pm1) and cubic pyrite-type 3D (Pa) phases of RhTe2 are metastable compared to a yet unobserved orthorhombic (Pnma) phase. This study unlocks the phase- and dimensionality-selective synthesis of rhodium chalcogenide nanocrystals and provides a foundation for exploring their structure-dependent properties.

item.title: Inverse Design of Optical Metamaterials Assembled from Plasmonic Nanoparticles
item.description: Self-assembly of strongly coupled plasmonic nanoparticles is a scalable and promising route for producing optical metamaterials with emergent photonic properties. Understanding, controlling, and designing the light-matter interactions of these components is crucial to improving their performance. In this paper, we formulate optical metamaterials design as an inverse problem, where we first specify a target optical behavior and then use numerical optimization to autonomously discover self-assembled nanoparticle metamaterials possessing the desired features. We use a coupled dipole method for electromagnetic simulation to efficiently compute gradients of optical figures of merit with respect to nanoparticle position, size, and parameters of the dielectric function analytically for gradient-based iterative optimization. Our design framework rapidly iterates through candidate materials self-assembled from tens of thousands of nanoparticles, and specifies the position, size, dielectric properties, and other physical features of each nanoparticle within an optimal metamaterial, subject to arbitrary constraints on the choices of design parameters. We use our tool to perform simulated annealing optimization to propose nanoparticles metamaterials with optical features tunable over an enormous range. In particular, we have inverse designed nanoparticle metamaterials with: 1) tunable extinction spectra of complex lineshape and 2) electric nearfield intensity with spatial profiles matching targeted patterns. By examining libraries of metamaterials with similar optical features, we can describe the key structure-property relations governing their optical responses.

item.title: Synthesis of Amphiphilic Polymer Co-Networks via the Growth of a Living RAFT Network. Part II: PEGDA-Based Parent Networks
item.description: This work represents the second part of our series on the synthesis of amphiphilic polymer co-networks (APCNs) via the growth of a living RAFT (reversible additionfragmentation chain transfer) network. In this work, we explore the photogrowth behavior of crosslinked polyethylene glycol diacrylate 700 (PEGDA 700) as a hydrophilic parent RAFT network. The model hydrophobic monomers—butyl acrylate (BuA) and methyl methacrylate (MMA)—were incorporated into the parent network via photogrowth, ultimately forming APCNs. The parent networks, daughter networks, and resulting APCN gels were thoroughly characterized using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), water absorption and dehydration, and swelling experiments.

item.title: Interfacial Assembly of 2D Superlattices and Quasicrystals in Binary Nanoparticle Systems with Strong Unlike Interactions
item.description: Two-dimensional nanoparticle (NP) superlattices assembled at fluid–fluid interfaces offer a versatile platform for creating novel materials with applications in plasmonics, spectroscopy, photonics, and catalysis. Recently, we implemented a basin-hopping Monte Carlo approach to identify ground-state configurations of binary NP assemblies at fluid interfaces, which helped predict a range of ordered superlattices, several of which have been observed experimentally. Here, we extend this approach by allowing unlike-particle interactions to vary independently of like-particle interactions, an experimentally relevant feature not considered in our previous work that captures systems such as oppositely charged or chemically dissimilar NPs. We systematically map the resulting phase behavior as a function of particle size ratio, NP-fluid interaction asymmetry, and unlike-interaction strength. The resulting structural transitions reveal how preferred immersion depths, geometric packing, and particle coordination collectively govern assembly. Strengthening unlike-particle attraction shifts phase boundaries toward structures with greater unlike-particle coordination, suppresses phase-separated and like-contact-dominated regions, and stabilizes new crystalline phases inaccessible when unlike interactions are constrained by the like-particle interactions. At strong unlike attraction, additionally varying particle composition gives rise to periodic approximants and quasicrystalline structures with 12-fold and 8-fold symmetry. Collectively, these results establish how particle size asymmetry, differential interfacial affinity, and independently tunable like and unlike interactions can be used to direct structural selection in binary NP assemblies at fluid interfaces.

item.title: Synthesis and characterization of polyazomethines – Towards a semiconducting paper
item.description: Novel organic semiconductor poly(azomethine) materials were synthesized via the polycondensation of terephthalaldehyde with two distinct diamines: para-phenylenediamine and 4,4’-diaminodiphenylmethane. These synthetic routes yielded a fully conjugated polyimine (P1) and a polyimine featuring a more restricted conjugation domain interrupted by a methylene spacer (P2), respectively. A comparative study was conducted to evaluate the influence of the conjugation length on some of their properties, mainly optoelectrical. Hydrochloric acid was employed as a dopant to enhance the electrical performance of the synthetized macromolecules. Furthermore, in alignment with eco-design principles to promote renewable and sustainable solutions, these polymers were integrated onto cellulosic supports either through physical deposition on cellulose filaments or via covalent grafting onto propargylated Kraft pulp fibers using copper(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC). Structural, morphological, and optical characterizations, including Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) and UV-Visible spectroscopies, solid-state 13C NMR, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM), confirmed the successful synthesis, functionalization, and fabrication of the biocomposite materials. Conductivity measurements and optical band gap (Eg) estimations revealed that the conformational flexibility of polymer P2 promotes tighter molecular packing and effective inter-chain interactions (π-π stacking), thereby enabling the development of bio-based semiconductor materials with promising potential for organic electronics.

item.title: Crystal-to-crystal solar energy storage in a hydrogen bonded dianthracene lattice retrocyclized by heat or e-beam
item.description: Solid-state (SS) systems for molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage are desirable for their simplicity and higher energy storage density compared to solution-based MOST systems, but it is difficult to design systems that both achieve high conversion to the metastable photoproduct and undergo thermally-driven release of the stored heat without melting. Anthracene (An) photocycloaddition to dianthracene (diAn) can proceed to high conversion in the solid state, but few crystalline Ans are appropriately aligned for dimerization, and even fewer diAns thermally retrocyclize without melting. By combining 9-pyridyl anthracene and 9-anthracenecarboxylic acid, we form hydrogen-bonded (H-bonded) and π-stacked chains that undergo high-conversion single-crystal-to-single-crystal photocycloaddition under simulated sunlight. Disordered packing in the lattice produces a mixture of the pyridyl-carboxylate “heterodimer,” the pyridyl homodimer, and the carboxylic acid homodimer. Calorimetry reveals that the H-bonded diAn product has a large separation between its thermal retrocyclization and melting temperatures, allowing the material to be cycled in the solid state. The H-bonded diAn lattice is also shown to undergo crystal-to-crystal retrocyclization under e-beam exposure. This work presents an easily-assembled all-SS crystal-to-crystal cyclable MOST system and demonstrates that H-bonding can be leveraged to increase the gap between thermal retrocyclization and melting.

item.title: A General Suzuki–Miyaura/[2+2] Photocycloaddition Approach to 2-Oxabicyclo[2.1.1]hexane Biaryl Mimetics
item.description: Herein, we report a modular approach to monosubstituted, (hetero)arylated 2-oxabicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes (oxa-BCHs). The strategy combines facile Suzuki–Miyaura cross-couplings to assemble suitable diene precursors that can undergo [2+2] photocycloadditions. Nineteen novel (hetero)aromatic building blocks and fragments are constructed from their respective (hetero)aryl boronates, conveniently accessed from commercial sources. Next, a high-throughput enabled synthetic sequence is performed, demonstrating the gram-scale conversion of 6-quinoline bromide to the corresponding 4-(quinolyl)oxa-BCH adduct. Finally, the physicochemical properties and aqueous stability of the new oxa-BCH biaryl mimetic was compared with those of other medicinally relevant substituents, demonstrating its promise as a robust, three-dimensional, polarity-enhancing motif for medicinal-chemistry applications.

item.title: Meropenem degradation does not necessarily eliminate antibacterial activity: responses of model and environmental bacterial isolates
item.description: Carbapenems can degrade rapidly in aquatic systems, and disappearance of the parent compound is often interpreted as loss of antibacterial activity. Here, we compared the antibacterial effects of intact meropenem with those of a meropenem mixture incubated for eight days in the presence of biofilm-covered moving-bed biofilm reactor carriers. During incubation, parent meropenem became undetectable, while several transformation products (TPs) retaining a closed β-lactam ring, a key structural feature for antibacterial activity, formed and persisted through the incubation period. The intact antibiotic and the incubated meropenem mixture containing TPs were tested against Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas fluorescens and two environmental isolates, CIS1 and CIR3, using optical density and viable cell counts. While intact meropenem strongly reduced viable counts of E. coli, P. fluorescens and CIS1, CIR3 was able to grow in its presence. In contrast, the incubated meropenem TPs mixture exhibited lower toxicity overall. Little or no TP inhibition was detected for P. fluorescens and E. coli, while CIS1 showed a weaker and time-dependent response. CIR3 was not suppressed by the mixture. Although the observed responses were subtle, the results show that disappearance of parent meropenem does not necessarily coincide with complete loss of meropenem-derived biological effects. The findings highlight that meropenem TPs should be considered when evaluating the environmental relevance of meropenem degradation and its potential contribution to selective pressure of antibiotics.

item.title: The pH effect in hydrogen evolution is a consequence of creating a solvated hydroxide ion
item.description: The hydrogen evolution reaction is orders of magnitude faster in acid than in base on the same electrode, a pH effect that first-principles calculations have not quantitatively reproduced. We trace this failure to the treatment of the ions: standard density functionals with standard solvation treatments undersolvate hydroxide–the ionic product of alkaline hydrogen evolution–by more than 1 eV against experiment and coupled cluster benchmarks, an error that tracks the functional’s self-interaction error. A screened hybrid functional with reduced self-interaction error yields Au(111) Volmer barriers whose acidalkaline difference falls within the measured range of onset-potential separations, whereas semi-local functionals predict zero to three times the measured value. Quantitative computational electrocatalysis therefore demands functionals benchmarked jointly against ion solvation thermochemistry and molecule-surface energetics.

item.title: Natural abundance isotopomics reveals coordinated amino acid metabolic alterations in human lung cancer
item.description: Background Metabolic reprogramming in cancer is usually characterized through changes in metabolite levels, yet pool size alone does not reveal how elements are routed through tumour metabolism. We investigated whether natural abundance isotopomics could resolve this metabolic organization in human lung cancer from bulk tissue to individual protein-bound amino acids. Methods Paired tumour and adjacent non-tumour lung tissues from 35 patients with non-small cell lung cancer (25 adenocarcinomas and 10 squamous cell carcinomas) were analysed for elemental composition (C, N, S) and bulk δ13C, δ15N and δ34S by elemental analysis–isotope ratio mass spectrometry, together with amino acid specific δ15N and δ13C and protein-normalized amino acid concentrations by gas chromatography–combustion–isotope ratio mass spectrometry. Changes between tumour and adjacent non-tumour tissues were assessed using paired statistics, correlation analysis, ANOVA-simultaneous component analysis and multilevel partial least squares discriminant analysis. Results Lung tumours showed a reproducible multi-isotope phenotype characterized by lower bulk δ13C and δ15N, higher δ34S, reduced N content and modest increases in C and S content. At the molecular level, glycine showed the strongest δ15N depletion and a parallel decrease in protein-normalized abundance, whereas proline and glutamate were relatively 13C-enriched. Glycine, proline and hydroxyproline concentrations were reduced in tumour tissue. Despite pronounced inter-patient variability, the multivariate tumour effect remained highly significant (permutation p = 0.0008), and multilevel modelling separated tumour from adjacent tissue with a cross-validated area under the curve of 0.922. Compound specific isotope changes were not systematically coupled to pool size, indicating that isotopic composition captures metabolic information not contained in concentration alone. The coordinated glycine, glutamate, proline and hydroxyproline responses further pointed to glycine related N handling and a glutamate–proline–collagen axis linking tumour metabolism to extracellular matrix organization. Conclusions Natural abundance isotopomics reveals a coherent metabolic phenotype of human lung cancer across C, N and S metabolism. By resolving bulk isotope signals into molecule specific responses, this approach identifies pathway level metabolic organization. This information is not apparent from level measurements alone. It highlights glycine metabolism and glutamate–proline–collagen remodelling as biologically relevant features of the lung tumour microenvironment.

item.title: The Role of Metacognitive Skills in Decision-Making using Type I/II Thinking
item.description: Strong reasoning skills are vital in a variety of academic and everyday contexts, requiring strong metacognitive awareness to be strategic and efficient. However, relatively little is known about how metacognitive abilities and skill-building relate to making purposeful choices about reasoning. We investigated the role of metacognition in Dual Process theory, including learners’ awareness and self-description of their cognitive engagement. Dual-process theory describes that most reasoning results from the interaction of two cognitive processes: Type I (fast/intuitive thinking) and Type II (slow/analytical thinking). The purposeful use of reasoning types is complex, including metacognitive awareness of the Type being used, identifying the optimal type, deciding if there is a need or benefit to switching, desire/motivation to switch, and the ability to do so (e.g., cognitive resources).
