This mixed-methods study examined how a metacognition intervention influenced awareness of and engagement with Type I/II thinking, and the impacts of training in discipline agnostic and discipline specific contexts (organic chemistry). Using an experimental design that included pre- and post-tests, participants completed a worksheet targeting Type I/II reasoning three times over two weeks. Participants in the treatment/intervention group completed a metacognition learning module, while the controle group completed an unrelated activity. In the worksheets, participants identified the thinking type they engaged with for questions and explained their thought process. We found that having an organic chemistry background and/or belonging to a particular group (intervention/control) were correlated with differences in analytical engagement. Participants in the treatment group demonstrated more deliberate monitoring and regulation of their reasoning, whereas participants in the control group relied on rigid, superficial distinctions between thinking types. Metacognitive accuracy and regulation varied across groups.

item.title: Divergent Two-Carbon Insertion of Alcohols
item.description: Carbon-chain extension enables systematic modification of molecular frameworks, yet general two-carbon homologation of alcohols remains underdeveloped. Herein, we report a divergent two-carbon extension of primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols through a radical–polar relay. Photocatalytic radical C–O bond cleavage merged with vinylsulfonium salt enabled a subsequent nucleophilic substitution to afford divergent two-carbon insertion products with oxygen-, nitrogen-, sulfur-, and carbon-based nucleophiles. The method tolerates alkenes, esters, carbamates, acetals, and complex molecular frameworks. Both two-carbon, and formal three-carbon homologation of alcohols are demonstrated. Intramolecular substitution provides substituted pyrrolidines or piperidine from amino alcohols. A quick access to fluspirilene, pimozide, and lidoflazine from 2,2-bis-4-fluorophenyl ethanol further demonstrated the synthetic utility.

item.title: Non-Isobaric Is Not Enough: Gap-Merge Safety for Unambiguous Peptide Readout
item.description: Selecting a set of non-isobaric amino acids is the standard way to guarantee unambiguous readout when peptide sequences are used to carry information. We show it is insufficient. Because tandem MS reads residues as differences between consecutive fragment masses, a single missing b/y ion merges two adjacent residues into one observed gap; if that merged gap aliases a single residue mass, the decoder does not register a dropout but emits one confident, wrong residue. Non-isobaricity cannot prevent this, because the colliding quantity is a sum rather than a residue. We formalize the missing condition—gap-merge safety, |m(a) +m(b)−m(c)| > τ for all a, b, c in the alphabet—as a decidable predicate with a machine-checked soundness proof in Lean 4, and characterize the collision structure of the proteinogenic alphabet exhaustively: beyond the Leu/Ile isobar and the Gln/Lys near-isobar, exactly two summed-gap collisions exist, Gly + Gly = Asn and Gly + Ala = Gln, making glycine disproportionately expensive. In simulation, alphabets satisfying gap-merge safety produce zero silent errors at every fragment dropout rate from 0 to 0.4, where alphabets chosen by non-isobaricity alone produce 1.0% to 6.9%; every failure becomes a detectable erasure rather than a silent substitution.

item.title: From Cancer to Infection: An amphiphilic ABAC Phthalocyanine for Versatile Phototherapy
item.description: The development of photosensitizers capable of operating across multiple therapeutic photoprocesses remains a major challenge in photomedicine. Herein, we report a cationic amphiphilic ABAC zinc(II) phthalocyanine (ZnPc-Me) obtained by a direct [3+1] mixed cyclization strategy followed by post-functional quaternization/transalkylation. The controlled amphiphilic architecture promotes optimal membrane anchoring while suppressing aggregation in lipid environments. Due to its optimized physico-chemical and photophysical properties, ZnPc-Me acts as a multimodal photodynamic platform whose biological activity can be switched between photodynamic therapy (PDT), vascular-targeted PDT, photodynamic inactivation (PDI) or photochemical internalization (PCI) by adjusting the administration, irradiation and dosing protocols. The compound exhibits high activity in cancer models (with EC50 in nM), surpasses clinically used photosensitizers under identical conditions, and retains activity in 3D tumor spheroids. In parallel, it efficiently inactivates multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens and enables photochemical internalization of a model drug through both light-before and light-after protocols, producing dose-dependent synergistic effects. Despite its high photodynamic efficacy, ZnPc-Me shows negligible dark toxicity, no hemolysis, and no epidermal penetration, ensuring a favorable safety profile for both topical and systemic applications. Overall, this work introduces a versatile design strategy for amphiphilic phthalocyanines that enables adaptive photodynamic activity across diverse biomedical applications, opening new avenues for the development of multifunctional light-responsive therapeutic systems.

item.title: Stereospecific Conversion of Alkenyl and Epoxy Carbamates into Cyclic Carbonate Alcohols
item.description: We have thoroughly explored the conversion of alkenyl and epoxy carbamates into cyclic carbonate alcohols. The substrate scope is robust, and the products are amenable to further transformations. In almost all cases, the reactions are predictably regioselective and stereospecific. The reactions can be run open to air and without precautions to exclude moisture. Indeed, H2O plays a critical role in the transformations and is added to the reactions as a key reagent.

item.title: Gas-Conditioned Message Passing Graph Neural Network for Permeability Prediction in Polymeric Membranes
item.description: Designing polymeric membranes for diverse gas-separation applications remains a critical challenge. Machine learning (ML) models can significantly accelerate this effort by capturing complex relationships between polymer-gas pairs and enabling permeability prediction over an extended chemical space of gases and polymers. In this work, we present a novel ML framework, the gas-conditioned message passing neural network (GC-MPNN), that jointly combines gas descriptors and polymer chemistry in a fused neural network model. Polymers are represented at the monomer level and encoded as molecular graphs, where node and edge information is propagated through message-passing layers. Six gas species (He, H2, N2, O2, CH4, and CO2) are represented using multiple descriptor sets spanning thermodynamic, kinetic, and electrostatic properties, along with one-hot encodings and combined feature sets that include kinetic plus thermodynamic descriptors and the full physicochemical descriptor set. For each descriptor combination, model hyperparameters are optimized using Bayesian optimization within a leave-one-gas-out (LOGO) validation framework. Test performance is then evaluated on the gas species excluded entirely from the corresponding training fold (out-of-training set) and compared across descriptor sets. For most gas species, the model achieves strong predictive performance (R2 ∼ 0.86–0.96), while CO2 remains more challenging in terms of absolute prediction accuracy (R2 ∼ 0.44). Active learning sampling further improves model performance by adding a few labeled samples from the test gas species into the training set. Among the three strategies tested, deep ensemble-based sampling and random sampling show strong improvement, with R2 reaching approximately ∼ 0.95 for all gas species, while evidential regression shows less consistent improvement. The model is further evaluated on a smaller polymer-gas dataset containing hydrocarbon species (C2H4, C2H6, C3H6, C3H8, and n-C4H10) using the GC-MPNN trained only on the six base gases, achieving moderate to strong Pearson correlations (r ∼ 0.77–0.89) for these out-of-training gases. Overall, this work presents a machine learning model that can learn transferable polymer-gas relationships from known gas species and extend them to previously unseen gases.

item.title: Symmetric versus asymmetric electron transfer in symmetric molecules
item.description: Photoinduced electron transfer (ET) in symmetric donor-acceptor-donor (D-A-D) or acceptor-donor-acceptor (A-D-A) molecules attracts attention due to applications in advanced materials. It is normally assumed that ET occurs asymmetrically, from one donor to acceptor, thus breaking molecular symmetry and resulting in a dipole moment in the excited state. However, the symmetry can be preserved with symmetric ET from both donors, leading to a nondipolar state with a high quadrupole moment. Here we report on symmetric ET in a D-A-D probe, 5,5'-di(9H-carbazol-9-yl)-2,2'-bipyridine. This probe is weakly solvatochromic in absorption, but highly solvatochromic in emission, revealing a nonlinear spectral shift and strong decay of the oscillator strength in solvents of increasing polarity. We develope a 3-excited-state model that fits the data quite well for symmetric ET, while no reasonable fit is possible for asymmetric ET. The model predicts the symmetric ET to be barrierless and ultrafast, in good agreement with observations.

item.title: Visible-light-Enabled O-Selective Radical Etherification of 1,2-Dicarbonyl Compounds for the Synthesis of Sterically Congested Ethers
item.description: A visible-light-promoted, triphenylphosphine-mediated protocol for the direct O-selective etherification of 1,2-diketones is reported. Using NHPI esters as radical precursors, this method provides an efficient route to sterically congested ethers under mild conditions. The strategy exhibits compatibility with various tertiary alkyl radicals and 1,2-diketone derivatives. Mechanistic studies support a radical-mediated pathway, and adaptation to a photochemical continuous-flow platform enables improved efficiency, scalability, and operational control.

item.title: Comment on “Charge Instability in Quadrupolar Chromophors: Symmetry Breaking and Solvatochromism” by F. Terenciani et al. (JACS 2006, 128, 15742)
item.description: We comment on the article by F. Terenciani et al., “Charge Instability in Quadrupolar Chromophors: Symmetry Breaking and Solvatochromism” (JACS 2006, 128, 15742). This article proposes a theoretical model for symmetry breaking and electron transfer in symmetric donor-acceptor-donor molecules, and reports experimental results to support the proposed model. However, our analysis demonstrates that their model is inconsistent with their experimental results.

item.title: Multilayer Multistate Reaction Coordinate Model for Nonadiabatic Dynamics in Open Quantum Systems
item.description: Simulating nonadiabatic quantum dynamics in complex condensed-phase systems is computationally challenging due to the high dimensionality of the nuclear environment. To address this, we introduce the multilayer multistate reaction coordinate (ML-MRC) model, a general hierarchical transformation of the multistate harmonic (MSH) Hamiltonian that maps the complex bath into a structured chain of collective modes. We demonstrate that the ML-MRC framework allows the MSH model to be reformulated into hierarchies of arbitrary depth, from single-layer reaction coordinates to full-chain representations, while maintaining rigorous mathematical equivalence. This flexibility is validated across diverse physical systems, including the spin-boson model, the Frenkel exciton model for the photosynthetic light-harvesting Fenna-Matthews-Olson complex, and a realistic photoinduced charge transfer model for a carotenoid-porphyrin-fullerene triad in tetrahydrofuran. Furthermore, this hierarchical structure enables a robust dimensionality reduction strategy, where truncating the chain yields low-dimensional effective Hamiltonians that accurately reproduce the nonadiabatic dynamics of the untruncated model at a reduced computational cost. Finally, the ML-MRC model reveals valuable mechanistic insights through reaction coordinate trajectories, which are shown to synchronize remarkably with electronic population dynamics across multiple systems.

item.title: Advancing Targeted Nanoparticle mRNA Delivery Using Machine Learning
item.description: Effective delivery remains a major barrier to translating nucleic acid therapeutics into the clinic. A successful delivery system must cross biological barriers, target the tissue of interest, deliver the potent payload to the cell, and be manufactured with ease at scale. The three clinically relevant carrier classes involve trade-offs with one another: viral vectors are limited by payload capacity and limited redosing; lipid nanoparticles are a clinical standard for mRNA delivery, but default to liver tropism; polymeric nanoparticles have lower immunogenicity and offer shelf-stable manufacturing, but fewer candidates have reached clinical trials. The design of effective nanomedicines requires multi-faceted optimization of nanoparticle properties, targeted delivery, and cargo efficacy. Machine learning offers an opportunity to accelerate nanoparticle development by effectively navigating the design space and providing a deeper insight into structure-activity relationships. Here, we present a high-level overview of the fast evolving nanoparticle delivery field and outline best practices for advancing the development of targeted nanoparticle mRNA delivery using machine learning. The key design principles are introduced: identification of target cell surface receptors, de novo design of epitope-targeted antibodies, design of mRNA payloads, and prediction of nanoparticle properties and their interactions at different biological scales. Together, advancing targeted nanoparticle mRNA delivery will require a coordinated integration of key design principles, the generation of high-quality datasets, and the effective adoption of machine learning.

item.title: Harvesting photosynthetic reducing power stored
Imaging of ultrafast electronic and chemical dynamics in biological systems
item.description: Ultrafast electron microscopy (UEM) has enabled real-space visualization of dynamics in inorganic nanomaterials on fundamental timescales, but its application to functional biological nanostructures remains largely unexplored. Here, we use time-resolved UEM and electron energyloss spectroscopy (EELS) to probe the photoinduced electronic response and the light-induced chemical modification of the conductive periplasmic nanofiber network extracted from filamentous cable bacteria. Low-loss EELS reveals a feature at 3.6 eV, assigned to π→π* excitations, that is absent in non-conductive bacterial controls. Upon femtosecond near-infrared excitation (800 nm, 4.8 mJ cm−2), the spectral weights of this π feature and of the collective valence excitation at 23.1 eV decrease by ~10% and ~8%, respectively, within the first ~2 ps and largely recover within a few picoseconds, leaving a small long-lived component. A comparison with the expected photothermal response indicates that this transient is dominated by electronic excitation. Power-dependent core-loss EELS and elemental mapping under quasi-continuous illumination show that cumulative exposure irreversibly depletes nitrogen and oxygen, relatively enriches sp2bonded carbon and causes partial mass loss, while the outline of the nanofiber network is preserved. These results establish time-resolved EELS as a probe of the electronic photoresponse and photostability of biological conductors, and show how transient electronic and cumulative chemical light-induced effects can be distinguished in such systems.

item.title: Depth-aware machine learning for 3D reconstruction of fibrous porous electrodes by FIB-SEM tomography
item.description: Quantitative three-dimensional reconstruction of porous polymers with sub-micrometer feature sizes is central to understanding and designing electrochemical interfaces and membranes. However, focused ion beam–scanning electron microscopy tomography combined with conventional segmentation techniques cannot readily recon-struct complex disordered morphologies such as fibers. Standard segmentation workflows misclassify out-ofplane material as in-plane material, distorting the reconstructed pore network, fiber connectivity, and interfacial area. Here, we introduce an annotation-free, depth-aware machine-learning framework that combines monocular depth estimation, trained on real-scale images, with unsupervised clustering to separate exposed polymer crosssections from subsurface contributions in serial FIB–SEM tomography images. Applied to copper-coated electro-spun poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene) fiber mats, the approach produces 3D reconstructions that preserve fibrous morphology more faithfully than conventional supervised and unsupervised segmentation. Quan-titative validation against capillary flow porometry, pycnometry, and high-resolution wide-angle X-ray computed tomography demonstrates improved agreement across pore diameter, fiber volume ratio, and copper-depth distribution metrics. This work establishes depth-aware segmentation as a transferable strategy from real-scale to nanoscale imaging, requiring no labelled training data and enabling accurate 3D segmentation and reconstruction from SEM images. This approach opens a path toward more reliable structure–property relationships in disordered porous polymer materials.

item.title: Optimal cyclic reflux operational policy for ternary mixtures separation. 2. Minimum boiling azeotrope mixture
Internally Polarized Covalent Organic Frameworks: A Design Strategy for Single-Component Photovoltaics
item.description: Molecular dipoles generate strong electric fields on the sub-nanometer scale, the very scale on which photogenerated excitons in organic semiconductors are bound. Harnessing such fields to drive charge generation throughout a photovoltaic material, however, has not been achieved. Realizing this would require ordering vast numbers of molecules throughout the bulk, which is precisely the structural control offered by covalent organic frameworks (COFs). In this work, we explore in silico the design of COFs that exploit internal-field-driven exciton dissociation, and show how they can be used to overcome a central challenge in single-component organic photovoltaics: converting strongly bound Frenkel excitons into long-lived separated charges. Using models that span from a single donor–bridge–acceptor unit to the full periodic material, we follow the photoexcitation process through its full cycle, from light absorption, through exciton dissociation, to charge recombination, and in turn isolate the effect of internal polarization at each stage. We show that polarization is essential for efficient exciton dissociation, preventing the kinetic hole trapping prevalent in an unpolarized analog. To investigate the recombination process on the nanosecond timescale, we develop a dedicated nonadiabatic molecular dynamics protocol, which, validated against an experimentally known donor–acceptor COF built from the same units, reproduces its charge-carrier lifetime with high accuracy. Applying it to the newly designed systems, we predict an almost 40-fold increase in charge-carrier lifetime. Our results identify internal polarization as a promising, unexplored approach to organic photovoltaic design and demonstrate how electronic-structure engineering at the building-block level translates into material-level performance.

item.title: How much of natural-product chemical space has a reference spectrum? An open audit of GNPS, MassBank and MoNA against COCONUT and LOTUS
item.description: Annotation of untargeted mass spectrometry data rests on reference MS/MS spectra, yet how much of documented natural-product (NP) chemistry actually has one has been asserted rather than measured. We present SPECGAP, an open, dependency-free engine that joins NP structure databases to spectral libraries on InChIKey identity and reports two quantities with explicit denominators: structural coverage, the share of reference structures with at least one experimental MS2 spectrum, and name-recoverability, the share of spectra whose declared compound name reconciles with the reference database. Applied to the complete open experimental layer—2,745,226 MS2 spectra from MassBank, MoNA and GNPS (280,024 distinct compounds)—against 738,823 COCONUT and 227,298 LOTUS structures, SPECGAP finds that 90.34% of COCONUT and 88.16% of LOTUS have no spectrum even when stereochemistry is ignored (exact-key coverage 2.86% and 5.08%). Coverage grows sublinearly: a 19.7-fold increase in spectra bought a 2.63-fold increase in covered structures, an elasticity of 0.32, because only 7.5% of the compounds in the layer are COCONUT natural products. Composition outweighs size: GNPS added 7.4-fold fewer new compounds than MoNA but a 5.9-fold higher NP hit rate (18.8% versus 3.2%). Both measures depend on the reference database: LOTUS is 3.25-fold smaller than COCONUT yet 1.78-fold better covered, while the same spectra recover 69.54% of their names against COCONUT and 36.17% against LOTUS. On the one run with archived match-level detail, 12.1% of recoveries came from fuzzy name matching; exact matching alone gives 31.82%, and we show the fuzzy rule can accept congener names. Library joinability differs 6.5-fold, and the GNPS MGF export cannot be joined at all. All code, audit outputs and derivations are openly released.

item.title: Plasmonic Monolayer MoS2 for Ultrathin Photoelectrodes in Neutral Water
item.description: Photoelectrochemical (PEC) electrodes can be used to create hydrogen to sustainably generate low-cost fuel and produce petrochemical feedstock. However, most semiconductors that drive the aqueous redox reactions in PEC devices cannot survive in neutral water, critical for widescale commercial production. Emerging, two-dimensional monolayer semiconductors can be electrochemically stable but generally do not capture enough sunlight to produce effective amounts of hydrogen. In this work, we propose a new PEC architecture that uses plasmonic enhancement to increase photocurrent in a monolayer MoS2 photocathode. By creating the first ZrN-based surface plasmon polariton (SPP) generator, we show fabricated nanostructures that plasmonically couple light with energies up to ~2.5 eV in water with near-100% light absorption. With transferred monolayer MoS2, the resulting Schottky diode demonstrates corrosion-free, fully stable photoactivity under 1-sun illumination in oxygenated, neutral water. We investigated and optimized the mechanisms of plasmonic enhancement, increasing photocurrent by up to 2.7x under AM1.5G illumination and 660% with wavelengths above the bandgap of monolayer MoS2. Furthermore, we show this architecture is compatible with standard roll-to-roll fabrication, and we use a technoeconomic analysis to estimate that levelized costs of hydrogen <$1/kg can be reasonably achieved with solar-to-hydrogen (STH) efficiencies of only 3.4%. Thus, with commercially scalable operational lifetimes and fabrication techniques, these results open the door to a new class of ultrathin PEC electrodes for economically feasible neutral water splitting applications.

item.title: Investigating the Antioxidant Potential of Annona muricata Leaves- An in silico Assisted in vitro Approach
item.description: Annona muricata is traditionally used in the treatment of various infectious and chronic non – communicable diseases. The antioxidant activity of the leaves of A.muricata was assessed using DPPH scavenging assay. The DPPH radical scavenging potential was compared with the proven antioxidant, ascorbic acid. The result of the study showed that methanolic leaf extract of Annona muricata exhibited the greatest antioxidant activity than the other three extracting solvents used. Six major phytochemicals present in A. muricata were taken from Dr. Duke’s Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical database and docked with Xanthine oxidase (XO) protein. Campesterol obtained the minimum binding energy value and hence maximum stability. The experimental results were in agreement with the docking results. Fifteen similar molecules of Campesterol were taken from PubChem and docked with XO which revealed that 2-methyltetracycloheptade-7-en-5-ol based scaffolds can act as potent XO inhibitors.

item.title: Multiscale modelling of acrylate networks
item.description: A systematic exploration of combining micro-to meso-to macro-scale models of crosslinking in three-dimensional polymer networks of Hexanediol Diacrylate (HDDA) is presented. Multi-scale modelling connecting realistic reaction kinetics from population balance (PB) models and network topology from molecular dynamics (MD) form the elements of the new modelling pipeline. Comparison of PB and MD predictions identify the initial radical concentration and model of initiation reactions as the principal source of discrepancy in species concentration profiles. They also largely account for the persisted differences in gel point and gel fraction predictions between PB and MD. Surprisingly, despite unavoidable widely different model conditions MD and PB find common ground in placing HDDA-gelation in a living polymerization regime. Two Random Graph methods are used to consolidate the inputs; the standard Configuration Model (CM) and the more recently popular Clustered Configuration Model (CCM) that incorporates self-cyclisation, double bond formation and small-cycles. It is found that CCM gives more accurate MDderived mesostructure than CM due to the better representation of neighbourhoods. Predictors for macroscale material properties consisting of degree of cyclisation, polymer-size distribution, and spectral graph measures are computed, with improved accuracy for the new CCM.

item.title: Old Drugs, New Targets: Multi-parameter computational prioritization of FDA‑approved, brain‑penetrant drugs as isoform‑selective GSK‑3β inhibitors for Alzheimer’s disease
item.description: Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β), a central regulator of tau phosphorylation and amyloid pathology, with its β isoform (GSK-3β) used as a main driver of the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) neurodegeneration. It is a validated therapeutic target in AD, yet no isoform-selective, brain penetrant inhibitors have reached clinical use. This paper screens 1000+ FDA-approved drugs by dual-isoform docking (GSK3α/β) and 8-seed redocking, prioritizing compounds by its α/β selectivity (G_select = G_GSK3A − G_GSK3B), CNS penetration, Hinge H-bonds, and pose plausibility. High selectivity alone provided misleading: filgotinib showed the largest G_select (+1.25 ± 0.03 kcal/mol), yet a reproducibly implausible pose, while abemaciclib (ΔG_select = +0.80 ± 0.09 kcal/mol; plausible‑pose fraction = 0.88) and peficitinib (+0.008 ± 0.02 kcal/mol; 1.00) provided a moderate selectivity with structurally reliable binding. Multi-seed redocking led to a hidden instability (loratinib plausible in only 25% of the seeds). This work provides a ranked, hypothesis-generating shortlist by establishing that isoform-selective GSK3β inhibitor discovery demands joint optimization of selectivity, and multi-seed pose stability, rather than affinity of GSK-3β alone. The following results are computationally prioritized candidates, rather than experimentally verified GSK-3β inhibitors.

item.title: Microstructure–Driven Degradation Mechanisms in High-Nickel NMC Cathodes for Lithium-Ion Batteries
item.description: Mechanical degradation in high-nickel layered oxide cathodes is closely associated with anisotropic lattice-parameter changes during electrochemical cycling, yet how cathode microstructure size influences the resulting crystallographic deformation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate two LiNi0.90Mn0.05Co0.05O2 (NMC955) cathodes with comparable secondary-particle sizes but different average grain sizes (1.0 and 0.5 µm). The fine-grained cathode delivers 30% higher initial discharge capacity, 40% lower voltage polarization, improved rate capability, and 13% higher capacity retention after 100 cycles. Despite its superior electrochemical performance, the fine-grained material exhibits approximately 1.23 times higher mean kernel average misorientation after 100 cycles, together with higher estimated geometrically necessary dislocation density, indicating greater average local lattice curvature. The coarse-grained cathode shows pronounced localization of crystallographic misorientation near grain boundaries and secondary-particle peripheries, whereas the fine-grained cathode exhibits a more spatially distributed misorientation response. Complementary chemo-mechanical simulations reproduce the grain-size-dependent trends in lattice curvature and reveal differences in the spatial distribution of plastic strain associated with the different grain sizes. After 100 cycles, the coarse-grained cathode undergoes extensive intergranular cracking and secondary-particle fragmentation, while the fine-grained cathode largely preserves its structural integrity. These findings identify the spatial localization of cycling-induced crystallographic misorientation, rather than its average magnitude alone, as a pivotal variable for electrode design.

item.title: Two extrapolation axes decide whether interaction needs a module in many-body systems
item.description: We separate the extrapolation problem in many-body systems into two axes: toward combinations with more components (the composition axis), and toward components unseen (the identity axis). The prevailing pipeline—encode then interact—performs poorly when extrapolating in composition count. We open an interaction-free route to interaction by strengthening its encoder until a component’s representation can carry what it contributes across the mixtures it appears in. Where component identities are bounded while their combinations are not, this route performs better along the composition axis, while the prevailing route is better along the identity axis; both differences follow from the functional forms rather than from the data. Chemical mixtures are the main example, synthetic tasks isolate the two axes, and the same structure recurs in other fields.

item.title: Light and magnetism in the origin of extraterrestrial enantiomer excesses
item.description: Chiral compounds are composed of non-superimposable mirror-images, or enantiomers, typically designated as D- or L-isomers. The macromolecular structures of biopolymers share a critical trait known as homochirality: the exclusive presence of a single enantiomeric form within their organic building blocks. Understanding the origin of biological homochirality has been an active area of research for nearly two centuries. Our goal was to demonstrate the first de novo synthesis of individual sugar derivatives containing enantiomer excesses (ee), the precursor of homochirality. We specifically employed prebiotically plausible experimental conditions: reactions were performed in aqueous solutions utilizing the formose sugar-synthesis pathway. This system consisted of simple, ubiquitous interstellar precursor molecules, such as formaldehyde and glycolaldehyde, alongside common abiotic ions, mild radiation, and magnetism. Analysis of products by chiral gas chromatography–mass spectrometry demonstrated ee production and, critically, reversible control of the dominant enantiomer by varying the magnetic-field direction. The ability to repeatably determine relative enantiomer abundance, and the ubiquitous nature of interstellar formaldehyde, magnetism and radiation, imply that ee might be cosmically widespread. These findings may also have implications for identifying the long-sought source of ee deeply embedded within extraterrestrial insoluble organic matter.

item.title: Editing-site selection for constrained QED improvement through frozen GenMol remasking
item.description: Shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph-attention models were trained on a remaskingsite selection task utilizing the GenMol generator and a subset of bioactive molecules (30,000 training and 5,000 validation) from the ChEMBL 37 dataset. Models learned to optimize fragment selection policies by maximizing the fraction of successful remasked candidates, with success contingent on an increase in the RDKit quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) under several chemical constraints. All three models show a marked increase in generation of at least one successful derivative out of 16 remasking runs on a held-out test set comprising 5,000 bioactive molecules: 66.0%–66.9%, 67.0%–67.4% and 66.3%–66.7% for the shallow network, boosted decision-tree and graph models, compared to 54.8%–55.6% for a fixed policy selecting the largest fragment (one-sided bootstrap 𝑝 < 10−4 for all models). A trivial baseline, selecting fragments randomly, displays 47.3% success. The fraction of valid candidates produced by all policies is about 99%. Analysis of learned policies showed consistent trends among the three models. Selection is biased toward larger pendants. Additionally, pendant selection shows several trends conditioned on the pendant-side, but not core-side, attachment atom. Larger carbon-and oxygen-attached fragments are selected more often (two-sided binomial 𝑝 < 10−10 in every model); a reversed tendency, albeit not statistically significant (𝑝 ≈ 0.02–0.30), is observed for nitrogen attachments. Controlling for fragment size, learned policies show preference for pendant-side nitrogen over oxygen and carbon, and for both chlorine and bromine over fluorine and carbon. Only LightGBM displays a statistically significant (two-sided exact binomial 𝑝 < 0.01) preference for sp2 over sp3 hybridization of pendant-side carbon atoms. At equal size, carbonyl-attached pendants are preferred to hydrocarbons.

item.title: A Redox-Switchable NIR II-to-NIR II Photoluminescent Vanadium(III/II) Redox Couple
item.description: Redoxluminochromic materials are useful for switchable optoelectronic devices that change the emission properties upon a redox stimulus. Typically, ON/OFF switches are realized, while materials with redox-induced changes of emission color are exceedingly rare. Here, we report a near-infrared II emissive vanadium(III) chromophore [V(tpe)2]3+ with an emission band peaking at 1110 nm. Its detailed photophysical properties including (ultrafast and long) excited state dynamics are elucidated by variabletemperature fs-ns transient absorption spectroscopy and luminescence spectroscopy. Together with its one-electron reduced counterpart [V(tpe)2]2+ (emission maximum at 1375 nm), we establish a proof-of-concept that d2/d3 spin-flip emitters can constitute redoxluminochromic materials, which switch luminescence from 1000–1200 nm to 1300–1600 nm in the very challenging near-infrared II spectral region.

item.title: Charge Donated by the Framework, Reactivity Expressed at the Metal: Tetrathiafulvalene-Programmed Nitrate Reduction to Ammonia
item.description: The decisive challenge in nitrate-to-ammonia electrosynthesis is not simply supplying electrons, but ensuring that successive nitrogen intermediates remain chemically convertible. Here, we establish a molecular strategy that differentiates framework-derived electronic character from metal-directed reaction selectivity through TU-420, a crystalline covalent organic framework integrating electron-donating tetrathiafulvalene and electron-accepting, metal-coordinating bipyridine units. Electronic-structure analysis identifies complementary donor-associated and acceptor-like states, while Xray absorption spectroscopy reveals distinct approximately six-coordinate Fe–O/N and four-coordinate Cu–O/N environments within the conserved architecture. Remarkably, TU-420-Fe achieves 98.1% ammonia Faradaic efficiency at −0.60 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and an ammonia production rate of 4.33 mg h-1 cm-2 at −0.80 V, whereas TU-420-Cu exhibits substantially lower selectivity despite its stronger cathodic response. Isotope-labeling experiments establish nitrate as the nitrogen source, while in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and differential electrochemical mass spectrometry reveal signatures consistent with evolving nitrogen–oxygen and hydrogenated nitrogen species. Density functional theory identifies the mechanistic distinction: Fe supports a favorable *NHO-mediated reduction sequence with a maximum uphill free-energy increment of 0.30 eV, while substantially alleviating the energetic penalty associated with the competing *NOH-mediated route relative to Cu. These findings identify the energetic fate of partially reduced nitrogen, rather than electron consumption alone, as a determinant of ammonia selectivity and establish electronically differentiated covalent architectures as platforms for programming metal-dependent multielectron catalysis.

item.title: Structural Order Reversed: Local and Average Structure Across the Ammonia Borane Phase Transition
item.description: Ammonia borane (NH3BH3) is a hydrogen rich molecular solid whose structural behaviour is governed by molecular orientation and N–H· · ·H–B dihydrogen interactions. Its temperature-dependent phase transition is conventionally described as an order–disorder transition from a disordered tetragonal phase to a more ordered orthorhombic phase. However, this description does not fully capture the underlying local structure. Single crystal X-ray diffraction, X-ray total scattering, Pair Distribution Function (PDF) analysis and Reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) modelling reveal an unexpected inversion of local structural order across the phase transition. At 300 K, despite pronounced disorder in the average tetragonal structure, the local structure exhibits three preferential NH3 orientations, whereas the BH3 groups remain substantially disordered. In contrast, at 100 K, modelling reveals substantial local disorder of NH3 despite the more ordered average orthorhombic structure. Single crystal diffraction additionally reveals weak satellite reflections, while the 100 K powder diffraction pattern is better reproduced by a trial commensurately modulated model with threefold periodicity than by the conventional average structure. Together, these results indicate that the low temperature phase combines periodic structural modulation with substantial local disorder, demonstrating that average and local structural order do not evolve in parallel with temperature.

item.title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts
The eventful journey of a ligand in and out of the binding site
item.description: The route a ligand follows to reach and leave a protein binding site typically involves complex molecular mechanisms that shape its efficacy as a biologically active compound. These mechanisms are reflected in the binding and unbinding kinetics, which often predict biological activity better than binding affinity alone, yet their calculation remains a bottleneck in ligand characterization. Here, we propose an approach that combines committor-based enhanced sampling with spectral analysis of the infinitesimal generator to characterize in detail how a ligand reaches the binding site of a protein and is eventually expelled. Applied to the paradigmatic benzamidine (BEN)–trypsin complex and the congeneric para-amino benzamidine (PAB), this framework reveals distinct and multifaceted binding pathways for the two ligands, uncovering a previously uncharacterized BEN binding site that competes with the crystallographic site, while identifying a common rotational bottleneck for unbinding. The computed unbinding free energies closely agree with experimental measurements. The spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator provides access to the slow dynamical modes of the system. From the slowest mode, we derive residence times and kinetic rate constants that agree with available experimental data and with independent OPES flooding simulations, while requiring substantially less computational effort. This approach offers a privileged perspective to resolve the complexity of protein–ligand binding-unbinding process, with potential applications to ligand screening and the characterization of multiple binding sites.

item.title: Resilience and regime change in refining margins: evidence from cointegration, Markov chains, and topological data analysis
item.description: This paper analyses the 3:2:1 crack spread over 20 years (2006 to 2025) using three independent methods: Engle-Granger cointegration, Markov chain regime modelling, and persistent homology applied to Takens delay embeddings. The data are publicly available EIA spot prices obtained via the FRED database. The objective is to determine whether the long-run equilibrium relationship between crude oil and refined product prices has survived the structural shocks of the last decade: the oil price collapse of 2014-2016, the COVID-19 pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and the addition of new refining capacity in the Middle East and Africa. Cointegration holds in 68% of rolling five-year windows, confirming long-run equilibrium. The equilibrium margin has shifted from $12/bbl (2006-2021) to $18/bbl (2024-2025). The error correction half-life has increased from 0.9 to 5.8 months, with the adjustment coefficient becoming statistically non-significant after 2017 (p = 0.38). Markov chain analysis discretises the margin into five regimes and provides N-step transition probabilities. The steady-state probability of normal-or-better margins is 55%. Topological data analysis reveals the most striking change: the pre-2020 crack spread exhibited 18 to 24 persistent homological cycles reflecting seasonal and inventory patterns. The post-2020 periods show near-zero topological complexity. The cyclic structure that made margins partially predictable for 15 years has not survived the combined disruptions. The three methods converge on the same diagnosis through independent mathematical frameworks. The practical implication is that prediction of refining margins is not impossible but conditional: it works when the market has topological structure, and it does not work when the structure is absent. The tools presented here provide a way to distinguish between the two regimes in near-real time.

item.title: Development and Evaluation of a Low-Cost Bio-Adsorptive Filter Insert (DrainGuard) for Stormwater Microplastic Remediation
item.description: Sub-millimeter microplastics (100–300 μm) in urban stormwater runoff represent a significant, unaddressed pathway for aquatic pollution. Conventional catch basins and physical interception methods lack the retention efficiency required to capture fine polyolefin fragments during high-velocity first-flush events. This study presents DrainGuard, a modular, decentralized storm drain filter insert utilizing a stratified bio-adsorptive matrix composed of biogenic cockleshell sand and agricultural coconut coir. A 46 mm inner diameter PVC column featuring a stratified bed (4 cm upper sand / 12 cm coconut coir / 4 cm lower sand) was evaluated at a baseline hydraulic flow rate of Qbase = 800 mL/min. Synthetic stormwater spiked with post-consumer polyolefin fragments (≈0.1 g) was introduced to assess mechanical capture efficiency and retention dynamics. Optical inspection (60x zoom) confirmed particulate interception and primary retention within the upper sand layer, with near zero microplastic detection in the post-filtration effluent, all while maintaining stable fluid transmission without rapid hydraulic failure. By repurposing low-cost, abundant biogenic materials, DrainGuard provides an accessible, sustainable, and highly effective framework for localized microplastic remediation in urban stormwater drainage systems.

item.title: Relativistic Bond Reconstruction in Chemical Bonding: An Information Dynamics Perspective on the CBi− Molecular Ion
item.description: In July 2026, the team of Lai-Sheng Wang at Brown University reported a landmark experimental observation in Science: the first direct spectroscopic evidence for the relativistic breakdown of the classical triple-bond picture in the CBi− molecular ion. Here we reinterpret this discovery through the lens of information dynamics—a framework that distinguishes between “real space” (wavefunctions and electron densities, where traditional quantum chemistry operates) and “virtual space” (defined here as the symmetry-rule manifold that organizes how real-space observables behave). We formalize virtual space as the set of irreducible representations of the Hamiltonian’s symmetry group, and show that relativistic effects drive a restructuring of this virtual space from the nonrelativistic C∞v to the relativistic C∗ ∞v double group. Four-component Dirac–Coulomb CCSD(T) calculations on CBi− provide the ab initio anchor: projecting the resulting spinors onto the symmetry-rule basis defines the coupling matrix Sij = ⟨ϕω i |ϕNR j ⟩ that connects real-space states to virtualspace rules. From this coupling matrix we extract a single input, the σ weight σ1 = 58.3% of the upper |ω| = 1/2 Kramers pair, and characterize the restructuring with the mixing parameter η, the label ambiguity A = ⟨H(σ/π|ω)⟩, and the mutual information I—the calculations supply the wavefunctions, while η, A, and I are outputs of the symmetry-constrained S-matrix model built on this one extracted input. A single-parameter constraint structure emerges: given the extracted σ fraction, unitarity enforces the complementary fraction and angular-momentum projection orthogonality enforces zero σ character in the |ω| = 3/2 orbital. We obtain η = 0.722, A = 0.453 nats, and I = 0.646 nats. The restructuring is a smooth crossover driven by the spin–orbit coupling strength λ, with η decreasing from 1.00 and I decreasing from ln 3 ≈ 1.099 nats in the nonrelativistic limit, the steepest change in A and I occurring near λ ≈ 0.4. All reported values are produced by a self-consistent, reproducible analysis pipeline, and are stress-tested by five numerical validation experiments (pairing-algorithm robustness, noise injection, subspace closure, the CN− null test, and a basis-set incompleteness model), which rule out numerical noise as the origin of the mixing signatures. Our findings demonstrate that the “anomalies” in heavy-element chemistry are not exceptions to existing rules but rather the manifestation of rule reorganization when the system crosses from the nonrelativistic to the relativistic regime.

item.title: Light-driven metal-free thiocarbonyl – olefin metathesis: a general route to sterically hindered alkenes
item.description: Highly substituted olefins are attractive scaffolds for molecular machines, optical materials and medicinal chemistry, whilst also serving as valuable intermediates in organic synthesis. However, their efficient and general preparation remains challenging, particularly in light of sustainability requirements. Here, we report a metal-free photochemical thiocarbonyl – olefin metathesis that provides access to a broad range of tri- and tetra-substituted alkenes, where light irradiation promotes both the regioselective formation and subsequent fragmentation of thietane intermediates. The scarcely explored photochemical cycloreversion of isolated thietanes was first thoroughly reinvestigated, leading to the proposal of a thioparabanate-photocatalyzed mechanism supported by Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TD-DFT) calculations. Then, the combination of this cycloreversion with a thia-Paternò_Büchi reaction into a photochemical cascade, enables the in situ generation of the thietane intermediate. Starting from thiocarbonyl substrates, independently prepared or generated in situ via Norrish type II fragmentation of phenacyl sulfide precursors, and diverse alkene partners, this light-mediated thiocarbonyl – olefin coupling offers an innovative and sustainable entry to a library of densely substituted olefins. The synthetic utility of this strategy is also demonstrated through its application to molecular motor templates synthesis.

item.title: Linear inductive bias boosts extrapolative molecular discovery by Bayesian active learning in the small-data limit
item.description: Bayesian active learning is widely used for molecular discovery, yet surrogate selection remains challenging when scarce initial data must guide the search beyond the observed property range. Here we benchmark diverse Gaussian process (GP) configurations across ten small-molecule and polymer datasets, focusing on the extrapolative regime where the initial labeled samples are drawn exclusively from below the median of the target property distribution. We identify explicit linear structure as an effective inductive bias for data-scarce extrapolative discovery: linear-kernel GPs provide a strong baseline, while adding linear components to a stationary kernel helps mitigate poor outcomes in the tail of the performance distribution. However, this advantage weakens under later-stage interpolative regime, where adaptive surrogate selection can further improve the discovery performance. These findings support incorporating linear inductive biases into data-driven materials discovery, where data scarcity and limited coverage of the design space are the norm rather than the exception.

item.title: Phytochemical Analysis and evaluation of the Antioxidant Activity of Cissus microdonta Planch.
item.description: Cissus microdonta Planch. is traditionally used to treat jaundice in Madagascar. This study aimed to investigate the phytochemical profile of Cissus microdonta stems and evaluate its antioxidant activity. Hexane (1.75%), ethyl acetate (3.74%), and ethanol (1.67%) extracts of the plant stems were obtained by maceration. Phytochemical screening was performed. The antioxidant activity of the plant was evaluated using the DPPH assay. Compounds from the active extracts were isolated using liquid chromatography on silica gel and identified via spectroscopic analysis. The presence of alkaloids, leucoanthocyanins, saponins, triterpenes, saturated sterols, and leucoanthocyanidins was established. The evaluation of the antioxidant activity of the ethanolic extract of the plant revealed significant free-radical-scavenging capacity. One compound was isolated from the active ethyl acetate extract and identified as ursolic acid. This research has enhanced the understanding of the phytochemical profile and biological properties of Cissus microdonta Planch., suggesting that the plant may be a potential source of natural antioxidants.

item.title: Balancing composition and phase stability in High-Entropy Metal Phosphates for proton conduction
item.description: The transition to sustainable energy technologies necessitates the development of proton-conducting electrolytes free from critical raw materials. Transition metal phosphate octahydrates (vivanite and pakhmoskyite analogues) offer a promising structural platform for proton transport via the vehicle mechanism, yet their performance is typically dominated by specific cation identity, with cobalt-based systems serving as the benchmark. This study investigates a high-entropy design strategy to decouple proton conductivity from cobalt reliance by stabilizing complex solid solutions containing up to several distinct metal cations (Ni, Co, Fe, Mn, Mg, Cu, Cd, Zn) within the phosphate octahydrate framework. Using a low-temperature aqueous precipitation method, we successfully synthesized single-phase high-entropy metal phosphates (HEMPs) and systematically evaluated their proton conductivity at 25 °C and 80 °C. While binary and ternary systems often require high cobalt concentrations to maintain performance, high-entropy compositions demonstrate a synergistic effect where increased configurational entropy correlates strongly with enhanced conductivity. Statistical analysis using Random Forest and ridge regression reveals that at 80 °C, configurational entropy surpasses cobalt content as the primary driver of transport performance. This entropy-driven enhancement allows for the significant reduction of cobalt to ~ca. 40 mol% without compromising conductivity, with optimised systems achieving values comparable to or exceeding the pure cobalt benchmark. These findings validate the high-entropy approach as a viable pathway for designing sustainable, high-performance proton conductors, demonstrating that structural disorder can effectively compensate for the reduction of chemically specific but critical elements in functional materials.

item.title: Site-selective alkali ion alloying in double perovskites via liquid-assisted mechanosynthesis revealed by solid-state NMR
item.description: Lead-free halide double perovskites with the general chemical formula A2B'B''X2 are promising materials for light-emitting and photovoltaic applications. However, compositional tuning of their structural and optoelectronic properties has focused on B-site and halide alloying. In this work, we show that Cs+ on the perovskite A-site of Cs2AgInCl6 can be partly substituted with Rb⁺ using simple apolar liquid-assisted mechanochemistry. By comparing Rb+ with Na+ substitution we show that ion size drives the site-selectivity of alkali ion substitution into double perovskites, with Rb+ and Na+ preferentially occupying the double perovskite A- and B'-sites, respectively. By combining multinuclear solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy with X-ray diffraction, we show that Rb+ not only enters the double perovskite site-selectively but also induces local symmetry breaking of the cubic structure, altering the optical bandgap and with potential implications for symmetry-forbidden photoluminescence emissivity. This work extends the tuneable compositional range of lead-free double perovskites to include A-site mixing while also establishing the site-selectivity of alkali ion speciation into the double perovskite structure.

item.title: PolyNet: A Python Package for Polymer Informatics
item.description: Polymers are used in a wide range of industries for diverse applications but formulating them to attain desired properties remains a challenging task. Polymer informatics has emerged as a powerful approach for the rational design of materials. Here, we present PolyNet, an open-source Python package that provides an end-to-end workflow for polymer informatics. PolyNet: 1) reads and validates datasets of polymer properties, including the monomer structures and their molar ratios; 2) creates vector- and graph-based representations of the polymers; 3) trains and optimises traditional machine learning (ML) models and graph neural networks (GNNs); 4) compares representations and models statistically; 5) deploys the models to screen in silico libraries of polymers, flagging polymers outside the applicability domain of the models and estimating their expected prediction error; and 6) interprets the models to understand structure–property relationships. PolyNet provides unique features such as: modelling of homopolymers and copolymers with any number of components, using the molar ratio of monomers in both vector- and graph-based representations; acceptance of textual representations of monomers or repeating units; calculation of polyBERT fingerprints and PolyMetriX and RDKit descriptors and fingerprints and accepting standalone user precalculated representations; benchmarking of all representation–model combinations on identical data splits using paired statistical tests; and chemically interpretable explanations through fragment-level attribution for GNNs and SHAP analysis for traditional ML models. Every experiment automatically records its configuration, data splits, hyperparameter search spaces and trained models, supporting full reproducibility in line with FAIR principles. PolyNet can be used through Python scripts, a command-line interface, or a graphical user interface for researchers without programming experience. We exemplify PolyNet by two case studies: glass transition temperature prediction for homopolymers, where cluster-based data splits showed that random splits overestimate model performance, the applicability domain identified less reliable predictions, and the model explanations recovered the known effect of chain mobility on Tg; and ¹⁹F MRI signal-to-noise ratio prediction for copolymers, where encoding monomer molar ratios is key to accurate predictions.

item.title: Crystallographic Visualization of Cooperative Molecular Motion Underlying the Photomechanical Response of a Diarylethene Crystal
item.description: Photomechanical molecular crystals convert molecular-scale photochemical reactions into macroscopic mechanical motion, yet how local structural changes develop into collective crystal deformation remains poorly understood. Here, we directly track the conversiondependent molecular motions underlying the photomechanical response of a diarylethene crystal, DAE-Et, by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Polarization-selective photoirradiation enabled the preparation of a series of photoreacted single crystals at different conversion levels while maintaining single crystallinity. Detailed disorder analysis revealed two distinct conformations of the closed-ring form, CI and CII, with the relative population of CII increasing with increasing photoconversion. Remarkably, the unreacted open-ring molecules also underwent conversion-dependent conformational reorganization from O toward O′, which correlated with lattice deformation and the macroscopic change in crystal angle. These results reveal the molecular origin of the characteristic induction period in the photomechanical response: photocyclization initially proceeds predominantly with the formation of CI with little lattice reorganization, whereas further photoconversion is accompanied by an increase in the population of CII and conformational reorganization of the surrounding open-ring molecules. Thus, the macroscopic photomechanical response emerges from intermolecularly coupled conformational reorganization involving both photoreacted and unreacted molecules. This work provides direct molecular-level insight into how local photochemical events are translated into cooperative motion and macroscopic mechanical responses in molecular crystals.

item.title: UPSTREAM: evidence-led, ledgered contribution to open metabolomics software, and what a corpus-wide name screen of MassBank found
item.description: Metabolomics depends on a small set of open projects—spectral libraries such as MassBank and GNPS, and processing software such as matchms and the RforMassSpectrometry packages—maintained largely by volunteers. Outside contributions can strengthen them or consume their maintainers’ time, and claims about how much someone has contributed are rarely verifiable. We describe UPSTREAM, a program that makes both problems explicit: every contribution must start from reproducible evidence and pass a ten-rule protocol, and the program’s headline count is computed from GitHub as merged pull requests only, never typed. We report the program’s first phase in full. A name-shape screen of all 139,006 records in MassBank 2026.03 flagged 1,480 names, of which 120 were defects (precision 8.1%), nearly all of them one collection’s internal identifiers. A name–structure screen that parsed 41,822 distinct names with OPSIN found 83,737 of 86,808 assessable records consistent (96.46%) and 3,071 candidate mismatches. Hand adjudication of 60 cases sampled from the two most suspicious strata found 58.3% to be screen artefacts, and confirmed 13 records (8 compounds) whose structure is a different compound from the one named; for six of the eight, the precursor m/z or the EI ions support the name. The same screen exposed a defect in matchms itself: clean_compound_name truncates 5 of 41,822 MassBank names, and a one-line fix truncates none. Phase 1 closed with 5 complete contribution packets (duplicate searches and author review still to do before filing), one item reopened when the target’s own documentation contradicted our premise, and two items closed because no failing case could be shown. The ledger stands at n = 0 merged contributions, because filing is the author’s step and had not yet happened. All screens, packets and derivations are openly available.

item.title: Balancing Plasmonic Response and CO2 Activation in Au–Cu/TiO2 Hybrid Photocatalysts via Alloy Composition Control
item.description: Plasmonic metal–semiconductor hybrid catalysts offer a versatile platform for solar-driven CO2 photoreduction by integrating efficient light harvesting with catalytic activation. Here, Au–Cu/TiO2 hybrid photocatalysts are developed as a model system to elucidate the role of plasmonic excitation and surface chemistry in governing CO2 reduction activity and selectivity. Alloyed Au–Cu nanorods with controlled Cu incorporation were synthesized and assembled with TiO2 nanoparticles, enabling systematic modulation of the Au/Cu ratio while maintaining constant metal and semiconductor loadings. The resulting Au–Cu/TiO2 interface functions as a tandem photocatalytic system, where Au promotes hot-carrier generation, TiO2 facilitates charge separation, and Cu enhances CO2 adsorption and stabilization of reaction intermediates. Under broadband illumination (350–2400 nm), pristine TiO2 shows limited activity, whereas Au incorporation enables the formation of formic acid, methane, and ethanol. Increasing Cu content significantly improves CO2 conversion while modulating product distribution: low Cu concentrations favor ethanol production, whereas higher Cu loading promotes formic acid and methane formation with enhanced hydrogen evolution. These findings establish composition-dependent structure–property–function relationships in Au–Cu plasmonic photocatalysts and provide design principles for controlling activity and selectivity in solar-driven CO2 conversion.

item.title: Halide Exchange via Perovskite Nanocrystals for Interfacial Defect Passivation in Solar Cells
item.description: Metal halide perovskites have emerged as leading candidates for next-generation optoelectronics, with perovskite solar cells (PSCs) achieving power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 26%. However, solution-processed hybrid perovskite films typically suffer from non-radiative recombination and ion migration driven by surface and interfacial defects, limiting device performance, fill factor, and long-term stability. To address these bottlenecks, we report a novel, scalable interface engineering strategy utilizing bromide-rich perovskite nanocrystals to modify 3D perovskite film surfaces via self-driven solid-state halide exchange. The resulting surface-graded heterojunction passivates key iodide vacancies, suppresses ion migration, and optimizes charge extraction. Consequently, modified PSCs demonstrate a ~5% boost in short-circuit current density () and an improved fill factor of 75.3%, driving a ~10% relative increase in PCE from 20.13% (control) to 22.19%. This simple, single-step nanocrystal treatment provides a promising pathway toward robust, scalable, and high-efficiency optoelectronic architectures.

item.title: Metal-Organic Framework Shells Limit the Intracellular Collapse of AC Hysteresis in Magnetite Nanocubes
item.description: Intracellular confinement suppresses the dynamic magnetic losses of nanoparticles after uptake, limiting their efficacy under alternating magnetic fields (AMF). A crystalline metal-organic framework (MOF) shell limits this collapse by enforcing a minimum interparticle spacing that restricts the dipolar coupling imposed by endosomal packing. A conformal UiO-66 shell about 9 nm thick grows directly on poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-silane-stabilized Fe3O4 nanocubes at room temperature without N,N- dimethylformamide, giving single-core nanocomposites. AC hysteresis measurements in A549 lung cancer cells show that internalization collapses the loop of PEG-coated nanocubes, which retain only 12% of their aqueous specific loss power (SLP) and 28% of their remanence ratio Mr/Mmax, whereas the MOF-shelled counterparts retain 40% and 47%. Recovering the nanoparticles from the lysed cells reopens the collapsed loops and restores Mr/Mmax to 81% and 89% of the aqueous reference, placing the origin of the loss in the spacing between cores rather than in their degradation. Under safety- compliant AMF, cells containing the nanocomposites lose metabolic activity, reaching 38% of the untreated control by day 7 despite a bulk temperature rise of 1 °C, a response absent in PEG-coated 2 particles at a matched intracellular iron load. Interparticle spacing therefore emerges as a design parameter for intracellular magnetic energy dissipation.

item.title: An experimentally-validated principle for selectivity in endergonic reactions
item.description: Selectivity between competing thermal reactions is, by textbook account, set either by the relative free energies of the products (thermodynamic control) or by those of the transition states leading to them (kinetic control). Neither principle applies to endergonic reactions: a non-equilibrium product concentration is maintained at the expense of an energy source, with species forming and decomposing simultaneously. Here we show that a third, distinct principle governs selectivity in endergonic reactions: the degree of turnover-frequency control, exerted by each intermediate of the kinetic barrier diagram associated to the reaction network. We demonstrate this principle experimentally, using a dynamic combinatorial system in which two furan derivatives compete for maleic acid in an endergonic Diels–Alder reaction driven by carbodiimide hydration. The product distribution depends on whether the system is at equilibrium or driven, and can be inverted under fueling. Kinetic measurements and analytical modeling quantitatively capture the observed selectivities – including counterintuitive non-monotonic responses – and recover thermodynamic and kinetic control as limiting cases.

item.title: Hg(II) Coordination in Human Thioredoxin Reductase 1: Molecular Insights into Mercury Toxicity
item.description: Thioredoxin reductase 1 (TrxR1) is an essential selenoprotein oxidoreductase and a sensitive molecular target of mercury, but the coordination chemistry underlying its inhibition by inorganic Hg(II) remains unknown. We use complementary Hg LIII-edge and Se K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected XAS (HERFDXAS), and density functional theory (DFT) to determine the Hg(II) coordination environment in inhibited human TrxR1. Se K-edge EXAFS provides direct evidence for Hg(II) coordination to catalytic Sec498 in wild-type TrxR1, with a Se–Hg distance of 2.44 Å. Hg LIII-edge EXAFS indicates predominantly two-coordinate, near-digonal Se–Hg–S coordination, with Hg–Se and Hg–S distances of 2.43 and 2.37 Å, respectively. Replacement of Sec498 by cysteine or serine gives bis-thiolate Hg(SR)2 coordination, demonstrating that Sec498 is not essential for Hg(II) binding. Hg Lα1 HERFD-XAS independently supports two-coordinate Hg(II) and distinguishes mixed sulfur/selenium coordination in wild-type TrxR1 from the bis-thiolate U498C variant. DFT calculations show that coordination by the adjacent C-terminal Cys497/Sec498 pair and structures involving the N-terminal redox center are compatible with spectroscopy, but do not unambiguously distinguish their relative energies. In contrast, bis-thiolate coordination in U498S, which retains only Cys497 at the C-terminal redox center, supports recruitment of a cysteine from the N-terminal site. These results directly characterize inorganic Hg(II) binding to TrxR1 and demonstrate how the strong, adaptable chalcogen coordination chemistry of Hg(II) enables it to target the catalytic machinery of this essential cellular redox enzyme.

item.title: Identification of Readily Accessible Manganese Catalysts Enables Multi-gram Scale Enantioselective γ-C(sp3)‒H Lactonization of Carboxylic Acids
item.description: Selective C‒H bond functionalization is a powerful tool to access complex molecules within a minimal number of synthetic steps, but its applicability on a large scale is often hampered by the requirement of harsh reaction conditions and costly catalysts. Among the existing C‒H bond functionalization portfolio, carboxylic acid directed C‒H lactonization has emerged as a particularly valuable transformation since it provides access to synthetically versatile lactone products from readily available carboxylic acids. Aiming at identifying catalysts that facilitate scalability of the reaction, herein, a collection of simple manganese complexes bearing triazacyclononane, picolinic acid, bipyridine and minimal N-based tetradentate ligands, which are established oxidation catalysts, have been screened in a model carboxylic acid directed C‒H lactonization reaction. While most of them proved ineffective, we identified two catalysts bearing simple N-based tetradentate ligands, Mn-(OTf)2(meb) (Mn-meb) and (R,R)-Mn-(OTf)2(mcb) (Mn-(R,R-mcb)), which are far more easily accessible than previously reported best-in-class sterically encumbered catalysts and provide lower yet still comparable performance under mild reactions conditions. Remarkably, high levels of enantioselectivity can be obtained in some relevant directed C‒H bond oxidation reactions. Even though these simplified complexes still operate in fluorinated solvents like hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP), we demonstrate that solvent usage can be minimized with respect to previously adopted protocols by working at up to 30-fold higher concentrations and recycling the solvent over at least three catalytic runs. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on a small scale using seven highly diversified substrates and on a five gram scale by the lactonization of a cycloalkyl carboxylic acid and a protected amino acid via secondary and primary C(sp3)‒H bond oxidation, respectively. More than two grams of a highly enantioenriched lactone could be isolated using only ~100 mL of HFIP, 1.5 equiv. of H2O2 and ~15 mg of an inexpensive and air-stable manganese catalyst (TON ≈ 1000).

item.title: DeNoMAP: An Interactive Web Application for Multi-Criteria Prioritization of De Novo Designed Compounds
item.description: De novo molecular generation is increasingly used in drug discovery, yet deciding which generated structures merit follow-up remains difficult, because established benchmarking metrics primarily characterize generative models rather than individual compounds. We present DeNoMAP, a general multi-criteria prioritization framework implemented as an interactive, open-access web application, which positions de novo-generated molecules in a normalized three-dimensional space defined by novelty, synthesizability and drug-likeness. A user-defined desirability zone enables transparent and reproducible candidate selection. Novelty is computed against ZINC20 as an external reference collection using the SmallWorld search engine, rather than against the generative model’s training set. Applied to a published library of 8,066 DNMT1 candidates, the web application identified 15 prioritized compounds among 852 successfully evaluated cluster representatives. DeNoMAP is publicly available at https://denomap.streamlit.app/ and its source code at https://github.com/flfeitosa/DeNoMAP.DeNoMAPDeNoMAP is a general approach to analyze de novo designed compounds obtained from generative models using multiple criteria commonly considered while designing libraries.DeNoMAPDeNoMAPDeNoMAP

item.title: Alkyl-BODIPYs as a Self-Photoredox Catalyst for their Oxidative Hydroxymethylation
item.description: The adoption of photocatalytic approaches for utilising small organic molecules in self‑catalysed reactions offers opportunities in green organic synthesis. We report that alkylated boron‑dipyrromethenes (BODIPYs) act as self‑photoredox catalysts for their own oxidation under mild visible‑light conditions. Using an imidazolinium salt (NHC-H) as a quencher, alkylated BODIPYs are oxidised cleanly to the corresponding hydroxymethyl derivatives in a one‑pot process. Luminescence studies, including Stern–Volmer analysis, support a reductive‑quenching pathway in which the NHC-H transfers an electron to photoexcited BODIPY to give a BODIPY radical anion. The method proceeds without external photocatalysts or stoichiometric oxidants and shows good functional‑group tolerance, highlighting the potential of these chromophores both as substrates and catalytic light absorbers. Moreover, the synthesized molecules were demonstrated to behave as effective passivating agents for layered Mn2+

item.title: An Analytical Full-Dimensional Potential Energy Surface for the H + C3H8 Hydrogen Abstraction Reaction: Non-Equivalence of the Primary Hydrogens and Variational Transition State Theory Kinetics
item.description: A new analytical full-dimensional potential energy surface, PES-2026, is reported for the gas-phase hydrogen abstraction reaction H + C3H8 → H2 + C3H7. It is built within the valence bond–molecular mechanics, VB-MM, framework and depends on 72 parameters, 65 of which were optimized against a focal-point CBS benchmark and against UMP2/cc-pVTZ geometries, harmonic frequencies and reaction paths. The surface describes the two chemically distinct abstraction channels, primary and secondary, and resolves them into three kinetically distinct channels: the six primary hydrogens are not equivalent, two of them being abstracted through an anti and four through a gauche saddle point whose adiabatic barriers differ by 0.26 kcalmol−1. Classical barrier heights of 12.05, 11.68 and 9.44 kcalmol−1 were obtained for the anti-primary, gauche-primary and secondary channels, reproducing the benchmark to within 0.04 kcalmol−1, and a relaxed two-dimensional torsional scan that did not enter the fit is reproduced with a root-mean-square deviation of 0.11 kcalmol−1. Thermal rate constants were computed between 200 and 1000 K with variational transition state theory and multidimensional tunnelling, CVT/µOMT, treating the three channels separately and summing them. At 300 K the total rate constant, 9.4×10−16 cm3 molecule−1 s−1, is 0.85 times the Tsang evaluation, and the calculated primary contribution, 5.6%, compares with the 4.3–4.7% derived from experiment and improves on the 9.5% of the most recent direct-dynamics study. Kinetic isotope effects are predicted for substrate and for attacking-atom substitution; the latter is inverse below ∼800 K, which is traced to the lowering of the adiabatic barrier upon deuteration of the incoming atom. The muonium analogue is also examined and is found to lie beyond the reach of a harmonic treatment.

item.title: Arsenite (Trisenox) Bridges the Redox Centers of Thioredoxin Reductase
item.description: Arsenic trioxide (Trisenox) is an effective treatment for acute promyelocytic leukemia and is being explored for broader anticancer applications, yet our understanding of the molecular basis of its anticancer activity remains incomplete. Under physiological conditions arsenic trioxide forms arsenite, As(OH)3, which has been proposed to target the thioredoxin system. Here, we investigate the structural basis of arsenite interaction with mammalian thioredoxin reductase 1 (TrxR1, TXNRD1), a flavoenzyme selenoprotein essential for maintaining cellular redox homeostasis. Arsenic and selenium K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, including highenergy resolution fluorescence detected (HERFD)-XAS, were combined with site-directed mutagenesis and density functional theory calculations. Wild-type TrxR1 forms a well-defined As(SeR)(SR)2 coordination environment in which arsenite binds the catalytic selenocysteine residue Sec498 and bridges the C-terminal and N-terminal redox centers of the enzyme. Replacement of Sec498 by cysteine yields an As(OH)(SR)2 species, whereas substitution by serine abolishes detectable binding. These results provide the first direct structural characterization of arsenite bound to TrxR1 and reveal a mechanism by which arsenite inhibits catalysis through crosslinking of the enzyme's redox centers. The findings establish a molecular basis for targeting of the thioredoxin system by arsenic trioxide and provide new insight into the chemistry underlying its anticancer activity.

item.title: A Highly Stable Cyclic (Amino)(Aryl)Nitrenium Radical Dication Exhibiting Temperature-Dependent Radical Bistability Maruti Suryavansi,a Manas Khatua,b,d Bappaditya Goswami,c Apurba Kumar Pal,a Subhas Samanta,*d and K. Geetharani*
item.description: Development of air- and thermally stable organic radicals remains challenging due to the highly transient nature of the free radicals. Herein, we present a strategy for isolating a highly stable N-heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) stabilized cyclic (amino)(aryl)nitrenium (CAArN) radical. This is the first example of a CAArN radical isolated in the solid state, and its identity has been confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and various spectroscopic studies. These CAArN radical exhibits remarkable stability towards air, water, strong acidic/alkaline conditions, aqueous buffers, and high temperature (~412 °C). The radical residing on two distinct redoxactive motifs exhibits unique temperature-dependent bistability in solution, as evidenced by VT-EPR and VT-UV-vis spectral studies. Polar solvents have played a crucial role in stabilizing the imidazolium motif, thereby facilitating the radical bistability. Further, by employing KC8, selective reduction of the NHC-moiety bonded to the CAArN radical was achieved to yield Thiele’s type hybrid diradicaloid.

item.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Subsequent Drug Release Trajectories using Early Release Information in PLGA Microparticles
item.description: Accurate prediction of drug-release behavior from PLGA microparticles may reduce the experimental effort required for formulation characterization, yet conventional prediction approaches rely primarily on static molecular and formulation descriptors and do not incorporate experimentally observed release behavior as it becomes available during an ongoing experiment. Here, we develop a machine-learning framework that integrates molecular and formulation descriptors with early-release measurements to predict subsequent drug-release trajectories from PLGA microparticles. A dataset comprising 4,913 release observations from 321 formulations was analyzed using random forest regression with formulation-grouped cross-validation. Using a common set of 89 formulations, we systematically evaluated the predictive value of increasing amounts of early-release information. Prediction accuracy improved with additional early measurements, but the incremental benefit progressively diminished, with two and three measurements capturing 64.7% and 91.9% of the total predictive gain achieved with four measurements, respectively. The value of early information also varied substantially across formulations, with greater benefits generally observed for formulations that were more difficult to predict from static descriptors alone.
